articles.title: The SS United States begins a final journey to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico
articles.summary: (AP) — An ocean liner that is longer than the Titanic and was once the fastest on the seas headed Wednesday toward its final home on the floor of the Gulf of...
articles.body:
DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — An ocean liner that is longer than the Titanic and was once the fastest on the seas headed Wednesday toward its final home on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico as the world's largest artificial reef .

The SS United States floated placidly under a cloudy sky off the coast of the Florida Panhandle, most of it still above the water at dusk, even after workers flooded the hull to push it under.

The event — described by officials as a controlled sinking — was a long-planned $13.5 million project aimed at attracting more divers and fishing enthusiasts to the area while creating a home for tuna, marlin and swordfish.

The process of sinking the behemoth vessel stretched through the entire afternoon and into the evening, despite predictions that it could happen in less than an hour once flooded. Smaller boats remained around and even up beside it.

The project will keep what had been a technological marvel when it made its maiden voyage in 1952 from becoming scrap metal. The ship's scuttling was streamed live online.

The SS United States crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times, carrying old Hollywood stars like Grace Kelly and Elizabeth Taylor. Other passengers have included Presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy and Britain's former King Edward VIII. In 1968, a young Bill Clinton took it when he went to Oxford University, decades before he was elected president.

Once aboard, passengers were treated to dinners that included caviar, roast duckling, smoked ox tongue and Calf's Head en Tortue.

In preparation for the sinking, organizers removed the 65-foot (20-meter) smokestacks and plan to have them anchor a new museum that celebrates the ship.

"We're not destroying anything," Tim Mullane, a Navy veteran and chief operating officer of Coleen Marine, the company sending the ship to the ocean floor, said in a video aired online by local officials. "It's going to serve a second life."

Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent Okaloosa County, Florida, and its contractor from using explosives to scuttle the ship, said Nick Tomecek, the county's spokesperson. Concerns about inclement weather prompted officials to move up the sinking by a day.

The SS United States has pipes that pulled seawater into tanks as part of the system that cooled its boilers, he said, and those tanks have been removed so that once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull. Workers also have cut 10-foot by 10-foot (3-meter by 3-meter) holes in the decks, and more than 400 portholes have been removed.

The ship is to sink in about 180 feet (55 meters) of water, with its top deck about 60 feet (18 meters) below the surface — shallow enough that inexperienced divers can visit. It will settle on the floor of the waters about 25 miles (40 kilometers) southwest of Destin, between Panama City and Pensacola.

Larger than the Titanic, the ship set a speed record on its first voyage

More than 3,000 workers helped build the SS United States in 1950 and 1951 in Virginia. An Associated Press reporter and Truman's daughter, Margaret, were among 1,700 passengers for the first voyage.

The ship's average speed for that trip was almost 41 mph (66 kph), besting a record set by Britain's RMS Queen Mary in 1938 by 4.5 mph (7.2 kph), according to the AP's dispatch .

The SS United States set the record even though its journey ended in the face of a full gale that reached 69 mph (111 kph) — "so strong it blew a ping pong table off the deck," AP reported.

At 990 feet (302 meters), the ship is 108 feet (33 meters) longer than the ill-fated Titanic, which hit an iceberg and sank on its first voyage across the Atlantic.

"She really embodies and expresses this country's best," said Susan Gibbs, the granddaughter of the ship's designer. "She represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty."

The ship's resting place has many artificial reefs

More than 500 artificial reefs are located in the waters near where the SS United States will rest.

Previously, the largest artificial reef came from the 2006 scuttling of an aircraft carrier, the USS Oriskany in the Gulf off of Pensacola — near enough to the SS United States site that an experienced diver could visit both in the same day, Tomecek said. The Oriskany, launched in 1950, was 911 feet (278 meters) in length.

"We're trying to be the best diving destination in the world," Tomecek said.

The ship was decommissioned in 1969. Attempts by a hotel magnate and Norwegian Cruise Lines to use the ship never floated, and from 1996 until recently, it sat along a dock in Philadelphia.

Mullane called the huge funnels — the smokestacks that have been removed to anchor the new museum — "works of art."

"I'm just so happy that we are able to save parts of her," Gibbs said.

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Eisenhower.

articles.title: A Rare Fish Found Underground in Death Valley Is Making a Comeback
articles.summary: Death Valley, California, a sprawling desert and one of the hottest places on Earth, is an unlikely home for a fish. And yet in a water-filled cavern that ex...
articles.body:
Death Valley, California, a sprawling desert and one of the hottest places on Earth, is an unlikely home for a fish. And yet in a water-filled cavern that extends deep underground, the Devils Hole pupfish is not only surviving, but growing in number.

The two-inch-long fluorescent blue pupfish are among the rarest fish on Earth and are classified as endangered because they are highly vulnerable to disturbance. The fish have been threatened by the overpumping of groundwater at nearby farms, which has lowered water levels inside Devils Hole, part of a limestone cavern that is more than 500 feet deep. They have also been imperiled by distant earthquakes that generate waves inside the cavern, dislodging algae that pupfish feed on. Reverberations from earthquakes in 2024 and 2025 reduced their population to fewer than 40 individuals.

Conservationists have sought to boost the ranks of the pupfish by introducing captive-raised fish. They have also provided the fish with supplemental feed made of mysid shrimp, water fleas, and blood worms. Their efforts are paying off.

In a survey conducted in the spring, scuba divers plumbed Devils Hole to tally pupfish. Working with researchers at the surface, they counted 77 fish. In the latest survey , undertaken last month, they counted 137, nearly double the earlier total.

Why are there fish in the desert in the first place? Some researchers speculate that the fish were carried to the cavern on rivers and lakes that converged in Death Valley during a wet period. Others think the fish were brought there by birds or humans.

articles.title: Scientists studying the Great Pacific Garbage Patch found that parts of the ocean brightened in blue and green wavelengths over 20 years; satellite data suggest tiny plastic particles may be changing its colour
articles.summary: Far out in the North Pacific Ocean, a floating mass of rubbish may be doing more than polluting the water.
articles.body: Far out in the North Pacific Ocean, a floating mass of rubbish may be doing more than polluting the water. New research suggests that these tiny plastic particles could be altering how sunlight scatters across the ocean, creating a subtle blue-green tint that satellites have detected over two decades. The particles responsible are too small to see from orbit. "We were shocked, excited, and a little alarmed to see the same shift in ocean colour on the map after we analysed the first satellite dataset of the garbage patch," ocean optics specialist Shea Cheatham of the University of Bergen in Norway told ScienceAlert. The findings of the study are published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.A garbage patch that's turning the ocean bluerThe Great Pacific Garbage Patch sits inside a slow, circular system of currents called a gyre, which gathers plastic from a huge area. Its size is roughly twice that of Texas. Despite the name, it isn't one island of junk. The debris is so thinly spread that satellites had never picked it up.Counting pieces gives a clearer picture. Tiny microplastic fragments make up about 94 per cent of the pieces floating there, yet they account for only about 8 per cent of its weight.Scientists at the University of Bergen in Norway, including Shea Cheatham, Daniel Koestner and Børge Hamre, didn't start with the sea. They first looked at how microplastics absorb and scatter light. Then they compared those properties with those of natural materials in seawater, such as phytoplankton and minerals. Their models suggested that the effect could show up at concentrations similar to those in the patch.Following this, they analysed satellite records from 2002 to 2022. Near the patch, they found a small but statistically significant brightening in blue and green wavelengths. Over the years, the water took on a gradually intensifying cyan tint, which matched the pattern their models had predicted."Our first reaction was disbelief, which is what led us to check two other satellite datasets just to convince ourselves that it was even remotely possible that we could be seeing the same signature evident in our models," Cheatham told the outlet.Plenty of things can change how the ocean looks. For instance, phytoplankton tends to make water greener, and dissolved organic matter can make it darker. Mineral dust can brighten the sea too, but it's more common in coastal waters. Measurements from a nearby research station showed that dust levels stayed steady during the study period. The researchers did find that certain natural changes could produce a similar signal. Those scenarios were rare in their simulations, though, making microplastics the strongest explanation.The current evidence points towards microplastics; however, it doesn't settle the question. Cheatham and her colleagues want to take optical measurements of seawater samples from inside the patch. "To fully answer the question of whether microplastics themselves are the root cause of this ocean colour shift, we will need to go to the garbage patch to make optical measurements of water samples and quantify the microplastics present," Cheatham said.So what can be done? Well, cleaning up the rubbish is a separate problem. Although trained professionals can pull out large debris, the tiny fragments are much harder to remove. Cheatham put it plainly: "At present, the only way to reduce microplastic pollution is to prevent it from entering the water in the first place."Microplastics not only change the ocean's colour but are also the "most likely to enter the base of the marine food web and end up on your plate", the researchers cautioned.

articles.title: In 2016, two vulnerable short-tailed albatrosses paired up on Midway Atoll near Hawaii; after 10 straight seasons together, George and Geraldine have raised at least five chicks, and their offspring are also returning
articles.summary: Some wildlife partnerships become remarkable not just because they last, but because they help bring a species back to places where it has rarely been
articles.body: Some wildlife partnerships become remarkable not just because they last, but because they help bring a species back to places where it has rarely been seen. On Midway Atoll in the North Pacific, two short-tailed albatrosses named George and Geraldine have reunited for their 10th consecutive year as a pair. The birds have successfully raised and fledged at least five chicks, and some of their offspring are now returning to the same island.According to a November 9, 2026, update from the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP), wildlife officials confirmed that George and Geraldine had returned to Sand Island in late October for another breeding season. The pair first appeared together on Midway in 2016 and raised their first chick during the 2018-19 breeding season. Their continued presence and the return of their young have raised hopes that the atoll could eventually support more breeding short-tailed albatrosses.How George and Geraldine became a pairGeorge and Geraldine are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus), a species classified as Vulnerable. Both birds were banded as chicks on Japan's Torishima Island, one of the important breeding locations for the species. They were first observed together on Midway Atoll in 2016. Their relationship eventually resulted in their first chick during the 2018-19 breeding season. Since then, the pair has continued returning to the same breeding area on Sand Island.According to ACAP, they have successfully raised and fledged at least five chicks. However, their breeding record has not been successful every year. They did not produce a successfully fledged chick during the 2024-25 season, but bred again in 2025-26. Their return in October 2026 marks the 10th consecutive year that the two birds have been recorded together on Midway, making them a familiar presence among wildlife observers monitoring the island's seabirds.Their offspring are returning to MidwayOne of the most encouraging developments is that George and Geraldine's offspring are beginning to return to the island where they were raised. During the 2025-26 breeding season, wildlife observers recorded eight different short-tailed albatrosses on Midway Atoll. Three of these birds were identified as offspring of George and Geraldine. This is significant because George and Geraldine remain the only established breeding pair of short-tailed albatrosses in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Although other individuals have visited the atoll, the presence of their offspring offers the possibility of a larger breeding population in the future.Young albatrosses do not necessarily begin breeding as soon as they return to their birthplaces. They can spend several years at sea before reaching maturity and establishing breeding partnerships. Therefore, the return of George and Geraldine's offspring does not mean a new colony has already formed, but it is an encouraging development for the species.Why the return matters for the speciesShort-tailed albatrosses are large seabirds that spend much of their lives travelling across the North Pacific. Their breeding populations are concentrated mainly on remote Japanese islands, including Torishima, where volcanic activity and other environmental pressures can affect nesting habitats. The species experienced a severe population decline during the late 19th and early 20th centuries because of commercial feather hunting. Millions of birds were killed for their feathers, bringing the species close to extinction. Conservation measures and protection of breeding sites have helped its population recover, although it continues to face threats. These include volcanic eruptions at breeding locations, storms, habitat changes and accidental capture in fishing operations. Because albatrosses spend so much time at sea, they can also encounter fishing gear far from their nesting islands.Midway Atoll provides an important location for observing how the species may expand its breeding range. Wildlife managers have previously used artificial decoys and recordings of albatross calls to encourage short-tailed albatrosses to visit the atoll and establish nesting sites. George and Geraldine's successful breeding history has made them particularly important to these conservation efforts. Their offspring returning to the island suggests that birds born there may eventually contribute to a growing local population.A possible beginning for a new breeding colonyFor now, George and Geraldine remain the only established breeding pair of short-tailed albatrosses in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. However, the eight individuals recorded during the 2025-26 season indicate that more birds are visiting the atoll, including three from the pair's own family. If these returning offspring eventually mature, find partners and begin nesting, Midway could develop into another breeding location for the species. Such a development would provide an additional population beyond its main breeding grounds in Japan.Their decade-long presence together is therefore more than a remarkable wildlife story. It also represents a small but meaningful step in the recovery of a vulnerable seabird, with the possibility that the next generation could help establish a lasting breeding presence on Midway Atoll.

articles.title: After examining 1,633 ancient skeletons from 30 sites in Peru's Lambayeque Valley, researchers found signs of violence in only 25 people, despite thousands of years of floods and episodes of ritual sacrifice
articles.summary: Ancient communities living along Peru's northern coast experienced devastating floods, food shortages and periods of mass human sacrifice, yet everyday
articles.body: Ancient communities living along Peru's northern coast experienced devastating floods, food shortages and periods of mass human sacrifice, yet everyday violence remained remarkably uncommon. A new study published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, also reported by science platforms Phys dot org and Scimex, has found that only a small fraction of people living in the Lambayeque Valley showed physical evidence of interpersonal violence over more than 3,000 years. The findings offer a different perspective on how human societies respond to environmental disasters, suggesting that climate-related hardship does not necessarily lead to widespread conflict. The research, titled Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, Interpersonal Violence, and Environment over 3,000 Years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru, was conducted by researchers Thomas J Snyder of New York University and Haagen D Klaus of George Mason University. The team examined skeletal remains from 30 archaeological sites, using evidence preserved in bones to understand how people experienced violence, accidents and environmental changes. Of the 1,633 individuals with sufficiently clear dates of death, just 25 showed signs of injuries associated with interpersonal violence. This represented approximately 1.6 per cent of the sample. Another 77 individuals had evidence of accidental injuries.The researchers then compared these findings with historical climate patterns, including changes in rainfall, water availability and the frequency of El Niño-related flooding. Their analysis found no significant relationship between environmental instability and either violent or accidental injuries. They also found no clear difference in the incidence of violence between men and women.A history shaped by extreme weatherThe Lambayeque Valley occupies a particularly vulnerable stretch of Peru's northern desert coast. Although the region generally receives little rainfall, its communities historically depended on rivers, marine resources and agricultural production for survival.This delicate balance was periodically disrupted by El Niño, a climate phenomenon associated with changes in Pacific Ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions. Particularly intense episodes can bring torrential rainfall and severe flooding to parts of South America. For ancient communities, these events could have devastating consequences. Floodwaters damaged settlements and agricultural land, while changes in ocean conditions affected fish populations and other marine resources.Archaeological evidence has also linked episodes of mass human sacrifice in the region to periods of extreme environmental disruption. Sites associated with the Moche and Sicán cultures contain evidence of large-scale ritual killings, which researchers believe may have been connected to attempts to restore balance between human communities and the supernatural world. These practices raised an important question: if environmental disasters were severe enough to prompt ritual sacrifice, did they also increase violence in everyday life? The latest findings suggest that this was not necessarily the case.Ritual sacrifice did not mean widespread violenceAlthough evidence of organised ritual killings exists at several archaeological sites, the skeletal record indicates that ordinary interpersonal violence remained relatively rare. The distinction is significant because ritual sacrifice and everyday violence represent different social practices. The presence of the former does not automatically establish that communities were experiencing widespread aggression, conflict or social breakdown.The researchers have suggested that access to marine resources may have helped Lambayeque communities withstand periods of agricultural disruption. Differences in how these societies organised their economies and social structures could also have played a role in limiting conflict. The study's findings also contribute to a broader discussion about the relationship between climate change and human behaviour. Research from other parts of the Andes has documented different patterns of violence during periods of environmental and demographic instability, indicating that communities did not all respond to hardship in the same way.What ancient bones reveal about climate resilienceThe researchers have cautioned that skeletal evidence cannot capture every instance of violence. Many injuries, particularly those involving soft tissue, leave no permanent marks on bones. The study also examined long-term patterns rather than individual events, meaning shorter episodes of conflict may not have been identified.Additionally, the researchers could not establish precise dates for every individual in the collection, limiting how closely particular injuries could be connected to specific climatic events. Nevertheless, the findings provide an important archaeological perspective on resilience. The Lambayeque Valley's history demonstrates that societies could experience repeated environmental disruptions without necessarily developing widespread interpersonal violence. Rather than treating conflict as an inevitable consequence of resource scarcity, the research highlights the role of social organisation, adaptation and access to resources in shaping how communities navigate periods of crisis.

articles.title: The Grand Canyon is missing over a billion years of rocks. Now scientists know why.
articles.summary: The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.
articles.body:

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion , which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature .

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament , a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics , said Shanan Peters , a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved. Nicolas Flament, geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Nicolas Flament, geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don't have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

articles.title: Scientists found a previously uncounted North Atlantic right whale calf beside its 38-year-old mother off Canada; the discovery raises the season's total to 24 babies for a species with only about 380 left
articles.summary: Scientists have confirmed that a North Atlantic right whale calf spotted off Quebec in September was a previously uncounted baby from the most recent
articles.body: Scientists have confirmed that a North Atlantic right whale calf spotted off Quebec in September was a previously uncounted baby from the most recent calving season, raising the season’s total to 24. The discovery, reported by the Associated Press (AP) and confirmed through analysis by the New England Aquarium, is a rare bright spot for one of the world’s most endangered large whales, whose global population is estimated at only about 380 animals.The calf was photographed beside its 38-year-old mother, a whale researchers know as Silt, near Anticosti Island in Quebec. Researchers with the Mingan Island Cetacean Study first recorded the pair, and scientists later matched photographs and data to determine that the young whale had escaped detection during the winter surveys normally used to document right whale births.A welcome surpriseNorth Atlantic right whales are so rare and so closely watched that researchers usually identify calves soon after they are born. The whales give birth in the warmer waters off the southeastern United States during winter, then migrate north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada as the seasons change.That makes the late discovery especially unusual. Despite extensive boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast throughout spring and summer, scientists did not see the calf until researchers in Quebec photographed it months later. Amy Warren, a scientist at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center, said the find was an exciting surprise so late in the year.Silt had been briefly observed in the southeastern U.S. calving grounds in February 2026, but researchers believe she may have given birth there and moved away before she and her calf could be documented together. The possibility that a mother and newborn could avoid detection for months is a reminder of how vast the ocean remains, even for animals tracked by dedicated research teams.Richard Sears, founder and director of Mingan Island Cetacean Study, said the discovery shows how easily whales can become lost in the open ocean. For conservationists, however, the calf’s appearance is more than a curiosity. It adds one more young animal to a population that cannot afford to lose many.A stronger calving seasonThe new calf brings the total for the most recent birthing season to 24, according to the New England Aquarium. That is the most productive season for North Atlantic right whales since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record, a result that offers cautious hope after years of alarmingly low reproduction.Successful calving years matter because the species has so few breeding females. Scientists estimate that only about 70 reproductive-age females remain, which means every healthy calf represents a meaningful contribution to the population’s future.The species has reached 20 calves in a single season only a few times since 2010. In 2018, researchers recorded no births at all, a devastating outcome for an already fragile population. Against that history, 24 calves is a significant improvement, even if it does not erase the longer-term decline.Right whale numbers have fallen since 2010, with the population losing about 25 percent between 2010 and 2020. The species has gained some ground since 2020, but scientists say recovery remains uncertain because the whales continue to face serious human-caused threats across their range.Why the species remains at riskNorth Atlantic right whales face two of the most persistent dangers in the ocean: collisions with large ships and entanglement in commercial fishing gear. Both threats can injure or kill whales, and both become more dangerous when animals move outside areas designed to protect them.Warming ocean conditions have made the problem worse. As prey shifts and whales alter their movements in search of food, they can stray from protected zones and enter areas where vessel traffic and fishing activity create greater risks. Conservationists say those changing patterns have heightened the dangers facing the species.The calf’s discovery does not change those threats, but it does underscore why researchers continue to track individual whales so closely. Because the population is small, scientists can identify many animals by distinctive markings and use photographs to follow mothers, calves and survivors of injuries over time.That close monitoring is also what made this discovery possible. The unidentified calf was eventually matched to Silt through photos and data, allowing researchers to confirm that it belonged to the current calving season rather than representing an entirely separate population of young whales.A reason for cautious hopeThe discovery is cause for celebration among scientists, but it is not a declaration that the species has turned a corner. A productive calving season can help a population recover only if calves survive long enough to reproduce, and right whales must still navigate shipping lanes, fishing grounds and warming waters.Conservation groups have criticized recent U.S. government decisions to delay new protections for the whales for a decade, arguing that commercial fishing interests have been prioritized over measures that could reduce entanglement risk. The AP reported that those moves have drawn concern from advocates who believe stronger safeguards are needed now.For now, the image of Silt swimming beside her previously uncounted calf offers a rare moment of good news. It is a reminder that even in a population of roughly 380 animals, the ocean can still hold surprises, and that careful research can turn an overlooked life into an important addition to the species’ future.

articles.title: Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile shut out Elon Musk’s phone service. Now the FCC is reviewing SpaceX’s plan to build its own
articles.summary: SpaceX could spend billions to take on Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile, as Elon Musk’s push into wireless aims to reshape America’s mobile market.
articles.body:
Elon Musk called it "the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX ) to provide complete phone coverage in America" — and it looks like the puzzle could be close to complete.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced on Nov. 10 that it had accepted a filing from Musk's Starlink Spectrum Holdings to buy 800 MHz Specialized Mobile Radio Service licenses from investment firm Grain Management.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The deal could come with an $8 billion price tag , as reported earlier by the Wall Street Journal. In a regulatory filing submitted in October, when the proposed purchase was first announced, SpaceX claimed it would "ensure all Americans have access to high-speed mobile broadband no matter where they go." In its announcement, the FCC agreed, noting that access, centered on cellphone tower wireless service, would be available to "approximately 100% of the U.S. population."

The deal could also add to the apparent concerns of the nation's three major carriers — Verizon ( NYSE:VZ) , AT&T ( NYSE:T) and T-Mobile ( NASDAQ:TMUS ) — who all reportedly rejected Musk's previous requests to allow his mobile service to piggyback off their existing networks. The companies, via CTIA, their wireless communications trade organization, also warned the FCC that a wider radio spectrum buildout could "have real consequences for consumers who rely on ever-increasing wireless capacity to access the modern economy and support their day-to-day living."

T-Mobile also appealed separately to the FCC, saying the quality of service in the 5G network could suffer if the agency makes more spectrum bands available. And in October, the three mobile carriers announced their own joint satellite partnership to expand coverage to "underserved areas" across the country.

SpaceX, meanwhile, spent $17 billion to buy spectrum from Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar — a deal the FCC approved in May.

A T-Mobile spokesperson told Moneywise, "We welcome competition because it pushes us to be better and creates more value for customers. Spectrum and towers alone don't make a network. Building a leading wireless network, providing top-of-class service and earning customer trust take significant time, investment and expertise. Satellite technology has an important role in extending connectivity, but it's complementary to terrestrial networks."

articles.title: New Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against SpaceX deal, says: Ready to have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but has a condition
articles.summary: Gina Hinojosa has set a condition for working with Elon Musk.
articles.body: ​Gina Hinojosa has set a condition for working with Elon Musk. Texas’ Democratic governor-elect, who campaigned against a proposed SpaceX land deal, says his companies must operate on terms that protect Texans’ interests. Her comments come as she seeks a pause on decisions involving state land near the company’s Starbase rocket launch site.​“We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies,” Hinojosa said in an interview with CNN after her election victory. “But it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor.” Her remarks leave room for cooperation while maintaining her objections to how the state handles Musk’s business interests.​What Gina Hinojosa said during her campaign​Hinojosa had criticised outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott over the proposed SpaceX transaction, arguing that public land should be protected.​“As Governor, I’ll protect our land and our livelihoods – not sell out to the highest bidder – because Texans deserve a leader who puts the people first,” she said in an October campaign press release. After winning the election, she asked the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department to hold off on further action during the transition.​“This morning I was pleased to talk to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife to confirm that this issue was not on today’s agenda and to request that no action be taken out of respect for this transition,” Hinojosa said at her first post-election press conference.​What the SpaceX land proposals involve​The state has considered separate transactions involving Boca Chica State Park, near SpaceX’s Starbase facilities in southern Texas. In March 2024, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission authorised negotiations to exchange approximately 43 acres of parkland for about 477 acres near the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge. The department’s announcement described the larger parcel as land for a new state park.​A separate August 2025 decision authorised the sale of four non-contiguous parcels, or plots that do not border each other, totalling about 1.9 acres. SpaceX wanted the lots for more employee housing, according to commission records. Department staff determined that these parcels had limited conservation and recreation value because they were located within an existing subdivision.​How Elon Musk responded​Musk defended Texas’ business environment in a post on X. He wrote, “SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government.”​“As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas,” he added.​However, Hinojosa’s transition team did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions about whether her position on the SpaceX negotiations had changed or what conditions could prevent the smaller land sale.Your child uses AI every day. articles.standfirst: Un misterio por resolver que, en algún momento, nos habremos interesado por la respuesta
articles.summary: Un misterio por resolver que, en algún momento, nos habremos interesado por la respuesta
articles.body: Las personas se habrán preguntado en alguna ocasión cuántos años le quedan al ser humano por delante o si viviremos para siempre. Pues bien, una investigación científica llevada a cabo por Bernt Bratsberg y Ole Rogeberg, expertos noruegos, analizaron la evolución de la inteligencia de varias generaciones de Noruega. Inspeccionaron los datos de 736.808 hombres noruegos nacidos de 1962 a 1991 y usaron las pruebas de capacidad cognitiva que se hicieron en el proceso de reclutamiento militar entre los 18 y 19 años. Observaron que estas puntuaciones medias fueron al alza hasta la generación de 1975, pero a partir de aquí, las puntuaciones de inteligencia fueron a menos. En definitiva, de 1975 a 1995 estimaron un descenso medio de 0,2 a 0,4 puntos. Esto refleja que la generación nacida después de 1975 es la primera que se ha registrado que tiene un cociente intelectual menor que el de sus padres. Actualmente, en el mundo entero, la población humana nunca ha sido tan elevada, con más de 8.000 millones de personas y al alza. En España, hoy día hay 49.935.642 habitantes, según reflejan los últimos datos del Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE). En este contexto, lo analizado por estos expertos noruegos quiere decir que cada generación de humanos es ‘peor’ que la anterior. Además, los investigadores afirman en su estudio que esto es un “peligro real” aunque parezca “increíble”. Por otro lado, Elon Musk aseguró que la especie humana podría extinguirse antes del año 2.100. Según el magnate, nuestra especie no podrá depender eternamente de un único planeta y defiende la colonización de Marte como alternativa. Por último, revela que las posibles catástrofes globales o el desarrollo de una IA super inteligente que podría escapar del control humano.

articles.title: Mysterious object moving through space could be lost Soviet probe as NASA weighs in on theory
articles.summary: Near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 shows nongravitational acceleration, and Harvard researchers say it closely matches lost Soviet spacecraft Phobos 1.
articles.body: A mysterious object speeding through the solar system is accelerating in a way gravity alone cannot explain, fueling a theory that it could be a Soviet spacecraft lost nearly four decades ago. Known as 1998 KY26, the roughly 36-foot-wide object is believed to be a near-Earth asteroid, but something other than gravity appears to be affecting its path. New research has now cast doubt on one explanation for what is pushing it through space. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman weighed in on the growing speculation Thursday morning on "Fox & Friends," saying some in the UAP community believe the object is making unusual movements, but he has seen no evidence KY26 is anything other than an asteroid. NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS' "First of all, nothing is about to hit us, to be very clear on this," Isaacman said. "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is a threat to our planet or anything other than an asteroid." METEORITE THAT CRASHED INTO NJ HOME HOLDS BUILDING BLOCKS OF LIFE, SCIENTISTS SAY Scientists refer to KY26's unusual movement as "nongravitational acceleration," meaning something besides the pull of the sun and planets is affecting its path. One theory has been that KY26 is a "dark comet" containing buried water that turns to gas and gives the object a push through space, even though astronomers have not detected the cloud or tail normally associated with a comet. But a new peer-reviewed study by Georgia Institute of Technology researchers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi casts doubt on that explanation. Their study, published in the journal Icarus, found KY26 is likely too warm for buried water ice to survive long enough to account for the unusual movement. The researchers concluded that calculated water-loss rates "preclude 1998 KY26 being a dark comet at present." There are other possible explanations. Previous research found that sunlight hitting KY26 and heat escaping from its surface could produce the extra push without buried water. HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING' Another group of researchers, however, has explored a far more unusual possibility. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and researchers Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl have examined whether KY26 could actually be Phobos 1, an unmanned Soviet spacecraft that stopped communicating while traveling to Mars in 1988. NASA SHUTS OFF VOYAGER 1 INSTRUMENT TO SAVE POWER 15B MILES FROM EARTH KY26 is about 36 feet across, reflects roughly 52% of the sunlight that hits it and completes a full rotation every 5.35 minutes. The researchers built a simplified model of Phobos 1 and compared the way it would reflect sunlight as it spun with observations of KY26. They found the spacecraft model closely matched eight sets of observations of the object. GIANT ROBOTIC CLAWS WILL GRAB DEAD SATELLITES IN SPACE They also tested whether sunlight pushing against a cylinder or solar panels could help explain KY26's movement and found the model better matched hundreds of telescope and radar observations. "Although an investigation of this kind cannot be conclusive," the researchers wrote, the findings "add strong weight to the Phobos 1 hypothesis." NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS The researchers stressed, though, that their model does not prove KY26 is the missing spacecraft, describing the theory as "strongly plausible but presently unproven." Other research points to a more conventional answer. A separate study published this year in Astronomy & Astrophysics examined the light reflected by KY26 and found its makeup appears consistent with a type of rocky asteroid. Researchers concluded it likely came from the inner part of the asteroid belt. Isaacman said NASA continues to monitor KY26 but sees no reason for alarm. SEND US A TIP "I have no reason to believe this is in any way remotely a threat to our planet or anything other than just an asteroid," he said. GOT A TIP? Scientists may eventually get a definitive answer. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Hayabusa2 spacecraft is scheduled to rendezvous with KY26 in July 2031, according to a 2025 study published in Nature Communications. articles.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI's natural gas ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.summary: SoftBank lost over $3 billion preordering natural gas turbines to power AI data centers. Here's what the loss means to power markets.
articles.body:
SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big.

Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess.

That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed.

The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects.

“SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva , told TechCrunch via email.

The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s . As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him.

Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless.

The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered.

“This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said.

The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar.

As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , told the Equity podcast Wednesday.

In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use.

Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected.

SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling.

The SS United States — a vessel that sailed across the Atlantic from 1952 to 1969 — was deliberately scuttled at around 10 p.m. ET on Wednesday, roughly 25 miles southwest of Destin, Florida. articles.title: House Republican invites Musk to move Tesla HQ to Florida
articles.summary: Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.) is asking Tesla CEO Elon Musk to move the company’s headquarters from Texas to Florida after Musk clashed with incoming Texas Gov. Gina Hinojosa (D) over a potential state land sale. “With the recent election of self-described Democratic Socialists to positions of power in Texas, I share your concerns about excessive…
articles.body:
Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.) is asking Tesla CEO Elon Musk to move the company’s headquarters from Texas to Florida after Musk clashed with incoming Texas Gov. Gina Hinojosa (D) over a potential state land sale.

“With the recent election of self-described Democratic Socialists to positions of power in Texas, I share your concerns about excessive government interference, politically motivated investigations, and policies that punish success,” Gimenez wrote in a letter dated Nov. 9 .

“No company should face political retaliation for creating jobs, investing in American innovation, and contributing to our nation’s prosperity,” he continued.

Musk spent millions of dollars to boost Republicans in the midterm elections, including donating $5 million to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) reelection bid, which he lost to Hinojosa. The incoming Democratic governor campaigned on a promise to pause data center expansion and won a court order to review unredacted versions of emails between Abbott and Musk.

Hinojosa has raised concerns about Musk’s business interests in Texas, particularly over a possible deal discussed by the state to sell Boca Chica State Park to SpaceX, which operates its Starbase facility nearby.

“As Governor, I’ll protect our land and our livelihoods — not sell out to the highest bidder — because Texans deserve a leader who puts the people first,” she said in a campaign release in October .

Following her election victory, Hinojosa said she had asked the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission to hold off on any action involving the potential sale until she takes office.

She has also signaled she is open to maintaining a working relationship with Musk and his companies, but she said it would have to be on her administration’s terms.

Musk, whose companies Tesla and SpaceX are both headquartered in Texas, argued the companies have prospered in the state because they were not operating under an “oppressive and extractive state government.”

Gimenez directly referenced those remarks in his letter, contrasting Texas’s incoming Democratic leadership with Florida’s Republican-controlled government.

“Florida offers a fundamentally different approach,” he wrote. “Our state has championed lower taxes, responsible regulation, and the freedom to innovate without unnecessary government intrusion. While others seek to investigate and punish success, Florida welcomes it.”

articles.title: Two German doctoral students were studying an unrelated reaction when their flasks filled with strange orange and yellow solids, and they had accidentally made molecules chemists had chased since the 1960s
articles.summary: A routine chemistry experiment has led to an unexpected breakthrough, helping scientists isolate a class of molecules that researchers had struggled to
articles.body: A routine chemistry experiment has led to an unexpected breakthrough, helping scientists isolate a class of molecules that researchers had struggled to capture for more than six decades. Two doctoral students at the University of Würzburg in Germany stumbled upon the discovery while investigating reactions that had nothing to do with their original research goal. Their findings, published in Nature Chemistry on October 27, 2026, offer a new way to produce stable oxoboranes, unusual compounds containing a triple bond between boron and oxygen. According to the University of Würzburg, the discovery came after two researchers independently noticed unusual orange and yellow solids forming in their laboratory reactions. What initially appeared to be an unexpected experimental result turned out to be a significant development in inorganic chemistry.A molecule that had eluded chemists for decadesOxoboranes have been on chemists’ research wish lists since at least the early 1960s. These molecules contain a triple bond between boron and oxygen, an unusual arrangement that has proved exceptionally difficult to stabilise. Boron is known for its tendency to form fewer and more varied bonding arrangements than elements such as carbon. Triple bonds are particularly challenging because of the element’s electron-deficient nature. While scientists had previously detected oxoboranes under extreme conditions, including in the gas phase and isolated matrices, producing stable versions that could be collected and examined at room temperature remained a major challenge.Researchers had also developed several related compounds by attaching stabilising chemical groups to the boron or oxygen atoms. However, these were not the same as isolating the oxoboranes themselves with their characteristic boron-oxygen triple bond intact. The latest research changes that picture. The team successfully prepared three oxoboranes that could be isolated as crystalline solids and remain stable at room temperature.An unexpected discovery in the laboratoryThe breakthrough involved doctoral researchers Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl, who were separately studying the reactions of a compound called diboracumulene with different ketones. Ketones are commonly used in organic chemistry and contain a carbonyl group, consisting of a carbon atom double-bonded to oxygen. The researchers were examining how these substances interacted with diboracumulene, a highly reactive compound containing two boron atoms.Instead of the products they had anticipated, both experiments produced unusual orange or yellow solids. Further investigation revealed that the unexpected substances were oxoboranes. The researchers found that the reaction could produce these molecules using relatively straightforward laboratory procedures. It also worked with different carbonyl-containing compounds, suggesting that the discovery was not limited to a single unusual reaction.The research team, led by Professor Holger Braunschweig, used experimental analysis, including X-ray crystallography, alongside computational studies to establish the structures and bonding characteristics of the newly isolated compounds.Why the discovery mattersThe significance of the findings goes beyond finally obtaining molecules that had remained difficult to study. Having stable oxoboranes available could allow chemists to investigate their properties and reactions in considerably greater detail. The three compounds displayed exceptionally short and strong boron-oxygen bonds, measuring between 1.208 and 1.217 angstroms. The researchers attributed their unexpected stability partly to the electron-rich chemical groups attached to the boron framework, which help reduce the vulnerability of the highly polar boron-oxygen unit. Initial experiments also showed that the compounds could react with amines, indicating that they are not simply stable structures but potentially useful starting points for exploring new chemical reactions.The Würzburg researchers are now investigating whether their approach can be extended to produce additional oxoboranes and other difficult-to-isolate compounds involving elements across the periodic table.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Meet the people who want peptides to be made in America
articles.summary: In this week’s Optimizer, we discuss a new movement to bring peptide production back to American soil in light of a recent HHS interim policy decision.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. We’ll be taking a break next week and will be back on November 25th. Opt in for Optimizer here. The SS Jeremiah O’Brien is a World War II Liberty ship. The hulking vessel was built in 56 days. It made 11 trips to Normandy, France, to supply the Allied powers in the fight against German U-boats. Last week, it was the site of a black-tie peptide party thrown by a trio of Gen Z venture capitalists. Roughly 150 people attended the event, where four types of peptide samples were provided to guests — no injections. One was a topical cream with GHK-Cu, while the other three were dissolvable sublingual strips from peptide startup Afterglow. GHK-Cu is a popular skincare ingredient, but it’s unclear how well sublingual peptide strips work. The topic of the night wasn’t just the state of peptides. The venue was a deliberate reference to American industrial prowess — and why the pharmaceutical supply chain ought to be centered in the United States. The timing couldn’t have been more pointed. Sourcing is one of the biggest question marks with gray-market peptides — something the US Department of Health and Human Services is trying to address with its recent interim policy decision allowing certain unapproved peptides for compounding. The decision is a controversial one. FDA career scientists haven’t endorsed it, though to the average person it might seem like they have. In fact, at a public hearing in July, FDA scientists categorically stated that there wasn’t enough evidence proving safety or efficacy for the experimental peptides in question. Some industry experts have cautioned that the HHS’s decision threatens the current clinical trial framework. By circumventing gold-standard clinical trials, it arguably allows telehealth providers and compounding pharmacies to bypass the approval process and create a parallel, dubiously regulated market. But for the party’s organizers Roxana Grunenwald, Yuva Krishnapillai, and Elia Ahmadi — all three are from Haus Fund, a biotech accelerator — this was an opportunity to make the case for American peptides. Hence the party on a wartime cargo ship, where guests left with stickers and hats emblazoned with “My Peptides Are Made in America.” [Image: Haus Fund’s Gen Z VCs talk “Biological Dynamism.” Listening to the three speak, they wouldn’t strike you as typical hooah patriots or MAHA activists — though there’s some overlap in their talking points. They’re venture capitalists promoting a certain viewpoint that’s trending in Silicon Valley right now. But it’s not just them making this argument. Hims & Hers — one of the most recognizable telehealth brands right now — is also hopping on the American peptide bandwagon. The push for American manufacturing is a thorny one. Last year, President Donald Trump’s tariff policies also reignited the American manufacturing argument, though the reality is it’s difficult to return to “made in America” after decades spent shaping the country into a services-based economy. Pharmaceuticals have also globalized. According to the US Pharmacopeia, 51 percent of all US prescription active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) comes from India and the European Union. China accounts for 10 percent. But when it comes to gray-market peptides, there’s a reason they’re commonly referred to as “Chinese peptides.” The vast majority of these research chemicals sold online come from Chinese manufacturers. “Right now, Americans are buying consumer peptides from gray-market sellers in China. And that concerns me because American consumers have little recourse if something goes wrong,” Ahmadi said in response to a panel question. “This is not a blanket criticism of China. This is not a criticism of Chinese people. America needs to be able to make its own medicines.” “I think this is a really good first step in solving the gray market problem,” Krishnapillai tells me, referring to the HHS’s interim decision. While building industrial infrastructure is a lengthy, complicated, and expensive process, he argues that this decision opens the door for compounding pharmacies to build a supply chain that adheres to US consumer safety laws. That in turn could give the FDA more insight into how to more effectively regulate the market. “The FDA [will be] able to see from a bird’s-eye view a lot more clarity, which will allow for structure to be built out and eventually a new path to API classification,” he adds. “We’re taking the stance that if people will be purchasing these peptides and taking them, sometimes even injecting, we want them to be American peptides,” adds Grunenwald. “We want them to be both compounded, produced, and verified on American soil.” “The hardware industry — semiconductors, the compute industry, electronics — have all recognized that the reliance on China for critical minerals is a huge issue. That’s very clear. The bio industry has not yet had that same pushback and the same epiphany about our reliance on Chinese APIs. We aim to bring this onshore. It’ll take a lot of money and a lot of time, but it’s not impossible,” says Grunenwald. For Ahmadi, onshoring peptides back to America is also a matter of regulatory consistency. “That made-in-America stamp is really only the beginning,” he says. “If we don’t have our own domestic production, we won’t be able to enforce our own regulations. Our markets are always going to be flooded by foreign imports and we won’t be able to have accountability to American consumers. So, we see this as the first step in a larger conversation to have America set the global standard for quality and safety in this new space.” Broadly speaking, these points have some merit. Several gray-market peptide users I’ve spoken with for an upcoming story stated that the mere act of importing “research drugs” and worrying about customs was a significant source of anxiety. That said, cost is another major reason why my sources tell me they opted to seek Chinese suppliers. It’s too soon to tell, but American-made peptides will likely be more expensive. That’s because an end-to-end US supply chain for these drugs is no easy feat. Even so, for some, that extra expense is worth it if it means signaling a higher-quality product. “We purchased an API manufacturing facility in California recently … Our intention is to leverage that capability to provide US-made API, and as a result, US-made product through the whole supply chain,” says Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer at Hims & Hers. The company purchased the facility last year, though it does partner with other companies globally to deliver compounded medications outside the US. [Image: Hims is launching Peptide Plus just as they purchased a new California manufacturing facility. But in this particular case, Vinjamoori is also specifically referring to Peptides Plus, a forthcoming service from Hims & Hers announced in the wake of the HHS interim policy. In a blog announcing Peptides Plus, Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum writes that the company “spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own U.S.-based peptide manufacturing facility.” At launch, the company plans to provide access to “Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable.” Notably, some of these substances, like vitamin B12 and NAD+, aren’t peptides at all. Meanwhile, sermorelin and glutathione are already legal. All of these, with the exception of BPC-157 and TB-500, are currently available through legal pathways. “I think it’s important not just to be able to say, ‘Oh, this is US made,’ but because it gives us direct oversight into the whole process,” says Vinjamoori, who says that he had prescribed peptides to patients in the past before the Biden administration moved certain research peptides to the no-compounding list. “Even then, there was inconsistency between compounding pharmacies. Everyone knew this,” he says, noting that doctors would individually recommend pharmacies based on what they were prescribing. “That to me, is still not ideal. That’s why we really felt it was worth making this investment — and to be clear, this is not easy.” When asked about how this might affect Peptide Plus pricing, Vinjamoori demurred, stating that the company would have more to share in “due time.” There are yet many unknowns with regard to the HHS decision and how it’ll impact the peptide economy at large. The decision is most notably an interim policy. It’s not necessarily a permanent or lasting change. It was also made before the midterm elections, so who can say how the policy winds will shift concerning tariffs and whether the zeal for “made in America” will fizzle as a result. But for now, it’s more than likely that you’ll start seeing some vendors touting that their peptides are proudly made in America. It’s entirely possible that they might imply that makes their product “safer.” That might be true with regard to sourcing and, to a degree, accountability. But it’s not the whole story. After all, in peptide America, sourcing is only part of the problem.

articles.title: Scientists have named a new orange-spotted fish under 3 cm long that lives in just three forest pools in Brazil’s Amazon, and they warn mining, plastic and deforestation may already have pushed it to the brink
articles.summary: What if you’re shopping for the perfect top for your night out and fall in love with this beautiful sparkly number, just to find out it is sold out in
articles.body: What if you’re shopping for the perfect top for your night out and fall in love with this beautiful sparkly number, just to find out it is sold out in your size? What I can only imagine would be tenfolds the amount of the same disappointment; scientists have discovered a tiny fish with orange markings, only to find out that the species may already be at risk of extinction.Laimosemion laranja, a dazzling little killifish found in Brazil’s Amazon is barely three centimetres long, wears bright orange spots along its body and bold chevron-like markings near its tail. It is beautiful, unusual, and, perhaps most worryingly, found in only three small forest pools.A fish unlike any otherThe discovery was made in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. Researchers from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará and the University of West Florida were surveying small rivers known locally as igarapés when they came across the fish. Its colour immediately stood out. Lead researcher Yuri Abrantes said the striking appearance of both males and females was unlike anything the team had encountered in the area before.At first, unusual colouring is not enough to declare a new species. Scientists need evidence, and plenty of it. The team examined the fish’s body proportions, counted its scales, studied skeletal features and compared it with closely related species. They also analysed mitochondrial DNA, which ultimately confirmed that this was not simply a colourful variation of a known fish, but an entirely separate species.A name rooted in placeThe name Laimosemion laranja is fitting in more ways than one. Laranja means orange in Portuguese, a nod to the fish’s vivid markings. It also honours Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.But the more scientists learned about where this fish lives, the less celebratory the story became. Laimosemion laranja has been recorded in just three small forest pools, and all three show signs of environmental disturbance. One pool sits near water discoloured by sediment linked to mining. Another lies within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the surrounding environment. Deforestation, mining and expanding urban development are all closing in on a species whose entire known range covers only around 25 square kilometres.That is an extraordinarily small home for any animal. For a fish that may depend on very specific forest pools, it is even more precarious. A single bout of pollution, a change in water flow, further clearing of vegetation or mining activity nearby could damage or destroy one of the few places this species is known to exist. The researchers believe the fish already meets the criteria to be classified as Endangered under the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s guidelines.Why this fish mattersAnd this tiny fish is more than just a pretty face. It belongs to a group of freshwater fish called killifish, some of which have evolved remarkable ways to survive in habitats that dry out seasonally. Their embryos can pause development and remain dormant in damp mud, waiting for rains to return and refill the pools. It is an extraordinary survival strategy, and studying species like Laimosemion laranja can help scientists understand how Amazonian killifish have evolved across Brazil’s varied environments.The Amazon is often spoken about as though it is endlessly full of life, and in many ways it is. But that abundance can create a dangerous illusion: because there is so much biodiversity, it is easy to assume there will always be more to find, more species waiting to be discovered, more time to protect them. The reality is far less comforting. Many parts of the Amazon remain poorly studied, and species may disappear before we ever know they exist. In this case, researchers at least found the fish in time to describe it, name it and raise the alarm. That does not guarantee it will be saved.What needs protectingThe research team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives. Protecting a species like this is not necessarily about building elaborate conservation projects; sometimes it begins with recognising that a small patch of forest, a few pools and the water connecting them matter enormously.There is also a broader point here about plastic pollution. Plastic waste reaches freshwater systems, including small forest pools in the Amazon. For a fish living in a habitat the size of a few puddles compared with the vastness of the Amazon, even local pollution can be devastating.Mining adds another layer of danger. Sediment can discolour water, alter habitats and disrupt the delicate conditions these fish rely on. When your entire world is a handful of pools, there is nowhere to escape to. There is no alternative population waiting elsewhere, no vast river system offering a safe retreat. The fish either survives where it is, or it does not survive at all.A future worth protectingLaimosemion laranja may be tiny, but its story is enormous. It is a reminder that conservation is about the species we may not even know of yet: the ones hiding in forest pools, under leaves, in muddy water and in places too remote or too small to attract attention. Sometimes, by the time we find them, the clock is already ticking.Scientists have given this little orange-spotted fish a name. Now the question is whether we will give it a future.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.
