articles.title: Researchers blasted discarded wind turbine blades with electricity at 2,000°C for half a second, turning difficult-to-recycle waste into a graphene-rich material that could strengthen new turbine blades
articles.summary: Wind turbines are often seen as one of the cleaner ways to generate electricity.
articles.body: Wind turbines are often seen as one of the cleaner ways to generate electricity. Their towering structures and enormous blades have become familiar sights across landscapes, harnessing something as simple as the wind to produce power. But what happens when these machines grow old? While generating renewable energy is one part of the sustainability conversation, dealing with the waste left behind is another.Wind turbine blades are built to withstand years of strong winds, rain, extreme temperatures and constant movement. Unfortunately, their durability also makes them incredibly difficult to dispose of once they reach the end of their working lives. Many retired blades are still sent to landfills, creating a waste problem that the renewable energy industry has yet to fully solve.Researchers at Tsinghua University in China may have found a rather unusual way to tackle this problem. They have developed a technique that uses an intense burst of electricity to heat discarded wind turbine blade material to around 2,000°C in just half a second. The process transforms the waste into two valuable materials, silicon carbide and graphene, which could potentially be used to make stronger wind turbine blades.Why are old wind turbine blades so difficult to recycle?Wind turbines generally have a service life of around 20 years. Once they are too old or damaged to operate safely, their blades need to be replaced. However, unlike many everyday plastic products, these enormous structures cannot simply be melted down and reshaped into something new.Most wind turbine blades are made using glass fibres embedded in a material called thermoset resin. The fibres provide structural strength, while the resin holds everything together. During manufacturing, the resin undergoes a chemical process called curing, which creates permanent molecular bonds. This makes the material strong enough to withstand years of mechanical stress, but also prevents it from being melted and reused like conventional plastics.Existing recycling methods have their own limitations. One common approach is pyrolysis, which uses high temperatures to break down the resin and recover other materials. However, the process can damage or weaken the recovered fibres. Mechanical recycling, meanwhile, involves shredding the blades into smaller pieces, which often limits how the resulting material can be reused.This leaves manufacturers with a rather difficult question: how do you recycle something that was specifically designed not to break down easily?A powerful electrical pulse transforms the wasteThe research team, led by Bing Deng, approached the problem by looking at what the blades were already made of. Their glass fibres contain silica, while the resin is rich in carbon. Instead of trying to separate these components and preserve their original forms, the researchers found a way to transform them into something else.First, they collected retired wind turbine blades from a wind farm in southern China and ground the material into a fine powder. This was mixed with carbon black, a form of carbon that helps conduct electricity. The mixture was then placed inside a quartz tube between graphite electrodes.The team used a technique known as flash Joule heating, which passes a powerful electrical current through a material, producing an extremely rapid rise in temperature. In this experiment, the mixture reached approximately 2,000°C (3,632°F) in just 0.5 seconds.At such high temperatures, the silica from the glass fibres reacts with carbon to form silicon carbide, a hard and heat-resistant compound. Meanwhile, the carbon from the resin reorganises into graphene, a material made up of extremely thin layers of carbon atoms. Graphene is particularly valued for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity.The result is a mixture of silicon carbide and functionalised graphene that can be recovered and used as an additive in fresh epoxy resin. Interestingly, the process does not require additional solvents or chemical catalysts to bring about this transformation.Could this make future wind turbine blades stronger?The researchers did not stop at producing these materials. They also wanted to find out whether the recovered mixture could actually improve the performance of new materials.They added small quantities of the silicon carbide-graphene mixture to fresh epoxy resin and tested the resulting samples for strength and stiffness. At an addition of just 0.3% by weight, the resin showed an approximately 11% increase in tensile strength and a 27% increase in tensile stiffness compared with unmodified resin. Its bending strength also increased by around 6%.The researchers found another interesting benefit. Adding just 0.1% of the recovered material increased the resin's thermal diffusivity by approximately 41%. In simple terms, this measures how quickly heat spreads through a material.This could be particularly useful for wind turbine blades, which operate in changing weather conditions. Ice accumulation, for instance, can affect their performance in colder regions. Materials that distribute heat more efficiently could potentially help address some of these challenges.However, it is important to understand that these improvements were demonstrated in laboratory resin samples, not complete turbine blades. More testing will be needed to establish how the material performs in actual turbine structures.A more affordable way to deal with turbine waste?Beyond the material itself, the researchers also examined whether the process could make economic and environmental sense.Their life-cycle assessment estimated that the technique could produce around 83% fewer greenhouse gas emissions than a thermal recycling route with heat recovery, and approximately 92% fewer emissions than chemical dissolution using nitric acid.A preliminary economic analysis also suggested that processing a tonne of discarded blade material could generate a net benefit of around $80. For comparison, the researchers estimated costs of approximately $460 per tonne for pyrolysis and $1,800 per tonne for chemical dissolution.These figures, however, are based on laboratory-scale assessments and modelling. They do not yet establish the actual costs or profits of running an industrial recycling facility.For now, the biggest challenge is scaling up the technology. Most experiments used very small quantities of material, with larger demonstrations reaching 10 grams. The researchers are working towards processing much larger quantities and testing the recovered material in actual turbine blades.Renewable energy is meant to offer a cleaner alternative to conventional power sources, but its sustainability cannot end with electricity generation. What happens to the infrastructure after it has served its purpose matters just as much. If this technique can eventually work on an industrial scale, discarded turbine blades may no longer have to be treated as the end of a product's life. They could become the raw material for the next generation.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: A critically endangered leatherback turtle tried to nest on an Ecuador sidewalk before finding a quieter beach; researchers tracked 146 eggs from her season and saw 134 hatch, a success rate of 91.8%
articles.summary: In January, under the light of a full moon and one too many streetlights, a critically endangered leatherback turtle named Bella did something both
articles.body: In January, under the light of a full moon and one too many streetlights, a critically endangered leatherback turtle named Bella did something both remarkable and worrying: she tried to nest on a sidewalk in Ecuador.Disoriented by nearby streetlights, the enormous female crawled over a rock breakwater and left the beach behind. She failed to lay her eggs there and returned to the ocean, still carrying them. Two nights later, she tried again, this time on a quieter stretch of sand at Playa de Crucita. There, she dug a nest, deposited 47 eggs, covered them carefully, and returned to the sea.A few weeks later, 44 hatchlings emerged and made their way toward the surf. Bella, it turned out, was only beginning. Researchers who had tagged her during her first attempt found that she nested four or five times during the 2026 season. Across all her nests, 146 eggs produced 134 hatchlings, i.e. a 91.8% success rate.For a species whose eastern Pacific population has fallen by more than 90% since the 1980s, that number is a small but powerful sign that leatherbacks may still be able to adapt, if people give them the space and protection to do so.A species on the edgeLeatherback turtles are the largest sea turtles on Earth, capable of reaching up to three metres in length and weighing as much as a tonne. They are extraordinary travellers: unlike most sea turtles, they thrive in both warm and cold waters, migrating thousands of kilometres from tropical nesting beaches to feeding grounds in cooler, subpolar parts of the Pacific, where they feed largely on jellyfish.But the eastern Pacific leatherback population is in serious trouble. Decades of fishing bycatch, plastic pollution, vessel strikes, egg harvesting and loss of nesting habitat have combined with climate-driven pressures to push the species toward collapse. Scientists warn that, without major intervention, the eastern Pacific subspecies could disappear within 60 years.Ecuador becomes unexpected habitatA new study led in part by Simon Fraser University marine eco-toxicologist Juan José Alava found a record-breaking number of eastern Pacific leatherback nests along several Ecuadorian beaches during the 2025–2026 nesting season. These beaches lie more than 1,000 miles south of the species’ usual nesting grounds in Mexico and Costa Rica.Historically, seeing a reproductive female leatherback on Ecuador’s coast was rare. Now, researchers believe the turtles may be adapting their reproductive cycles to take advantage of Ecuador’s coastline, particularly during cooler La Niña periods in the southeastern tropical Pacific.The researchers reviewed more than 45 years of records, including sightings of adult females, nests, hatching success, nesting attempts and strandings. They compared these records with El Niño and La Niña events, which cause major swings in sea-surface temperatures.They found that leatherback activity and nesting in Ecuador increased during cooler La Niña episodes over the past decade. Even more importantly, the number of eggs per nest and hatching rates in Ecuador were comparable to those in the turtles’ traditional nesting grounds. In some cases, Ecuadorian nests produced more hatchlings than usual.That does not mean climate change is good for leatherbacks. Rather, it suggests that some turtles may be responding to warming and shifting ocean conditions by seeking out cooler coastal areas where reproduction can still succeed. It is adaptation, but it is also a warning: species are being forced to move, and their survival depends on whether the places they move to remain safe.Bella’s first failed nesting attempt reveals another side of the problem. Leatherbacks are powerful swimmers, but on land they are vulnerable, slow and easily confused. Artificial lighting can disorient nesting females and hatchlings, drawing them away from the ocean and toward roads, buildings and other hazards.When Bella encountered streetlights near Playa de Crucita, she left the beach and climbed onto a sidewalk. Had conditions been different, she could have been injured, stranded, or unable to lay her eggs at all. Instead, she returned to the sea and found a quieter location two nights later.Conservation thus includes managing the everyday edges of coastal towns: reducing light pollution, keeping beaches clear and accessible, controlling vehicle access, and ensuring that nesting females are not disturbed.From hatchlings to hopeEcuador’s role in leatherback conservation is not entirely new. In 2021, nine leatherbacks hatched after their eggs were artificially incubated at Punta Bikini beach in Manabí province. Earlier that year, 60 leatherbacks had also hatched in the region. Before those successes, nests found along the Ecuadorian coast in 2015 and 2017 had not produced hatchlings.The difference now is scale and consistency. Bella’s 91.8% hatching success, alongside the wider increase in nesting activity, suggests that Ecuador may be becoming more than an occasional stopover. It may be emerging as a meaningful secondary nesting area for a population that desperately needs options.Still, researchers caution against treating this as a victory lap. A good nesting season cannot undo decades of decline. Leatherbacks face dangers long before they reach a beach and long after hatchlings enter the water: fishing nets, plastic debris, boat traffic, changing food supplies and warming oceans all remain serious threats.What needs to happen nextThe study’s authors argue that protecting Ecuador’s beaches must become a priority. That means sustained monitoring, effective coastal-zone management, efforts to reduce fishing bycatch, and conservation plans developed with local communities and Indigenous and traditional knowledge holders.It also means protecting the conditions that made Bella’s second attempt successful: dark, quiet beaches; safe nesting habitat; and hatcheries or relocation programmes only when genuinely necessary. Conservation works best when it supports natural behaviour rather than replacing it.Bella’s 134 hatchlings are not guaranteed to survive. Many will face predators, fishing gear, pollution and an ocean that is changing faster than evolution can comfortably respond. But their emergence is proof that the species is not finished yet.A turtle that briefly mistook a sidewalk for a nesting beach, then found her way back to the sand, has given scientists and conservationists something rare: hope grounded in evidence. The challenge now is to make sure that, next nesting season, Bella and turtles like her find safe beaches waiting for them, not lights, roads and obstacles.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: SpaceX Starship test to attempt first-ever spaceship 'catch'
articles.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX was poised Friday to carry out its latest test of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, the Starship, with plans for a groundbreak...
articles.body:
Elon Musk's SpaceX was poised Friday to carry out its latest test of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, the Starship, with plans for a groundbreaking "catch" of the spaceship following a day in orbit.

A successful capture of the Starship upper stage would mark a significant milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable spacecraft that can drastically reduce mission costs and make frequent travel possible.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX said.

For the 15th Starship test flight Friday, SpaceX aims to recover both stages of the massive 124-meter (407-foot) launch vehicle.

The company has caught the booster, dubbed Super Heavy, on three previous occasions, with the first stage descending vertically back to the launch site shortly after blastoff and nestling into mechanical "chopstick" arms.

It will now attempt to do the same with the spaceship. Some versions of the vessel are designed to launch internet satellites and data centers into orbit, while others will be made to ferry people to the Moon and Mars.

A spacecraft that can be fully reused is the "Holy Grail" of the space industry, said Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

"No one's really been able to do that so far," he said. "People have been trying to do that since the (NASA) space shuttle. But the space shuttle ended up being kind of a compromise because a lot of the vehicle wasn't reusable."

Reusing the Starship spacecraft would require the vessel to withstand the extreme heat of reentering Earth's atmosphere and then return to service without extensive refurbishment.

Musk, the world's richest person, has already revolutionized the space sector with the partially reusable Falcon rockets, which are regularly employed to launch satellites and carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

The Starship project, however, has been plagued by years-long delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges -- even as NASA is counting on the spaceship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program.

Other technical challenges include transferring fuel to Starship in orbit -- a requirement for any journey to the Moon or Mars.

Following SpaceX's high-profile stock market debut in June, the company carried out the first orbital flight of Starship in September, though the mission was cut short due to an engine issue.

It is also investing heavily in additional launch sites for its mega-rocket in Louisiana and Florida.

Friday's launch is scheduled to take place at SpaceX's "Starbase" in southern Texas at 4:45 pm (2245 GMT).

Following liftoff and the mid-air separation of the two stages, SpaceX plans to bring Super Heavy back to Earth six and a half minutes later, catching it at the launch site on the Gulf of Mexico coastline.

The spaceship will continue to reach Earth's orbit, where it will deploy 26 satellites into Musk's Starlink satellite internet constellation that has become a major revenue stream for SpaceX.

It will then circle the planet 14 times, before returning 22 hours later and -- SpaceX hopes -- descending safely into the chopstick arms.

This capture attempt is more complex than that of the booster, as the spaceship will be descending much faster and from a much greater altitude.

SpaceX has said it would proceed with these maneuvers only if conditions are optimal, and in the past has made last-minute changes to test flights under Musk's "fail fast" strategy of learning through crashes, explosions and other mishaps.

As of late Thursday, the US Federal Aviation Administration had not yet given its final approval for the test flight.

articles.summary: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has announced its plans to invest more than $74 billion in to of its artificial intelligence computing campuses in Texas and Arizona.
articles.body: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has announced its plans to invest more than $74 billion in to of its artificial intelligence computing campuses in Texas and Arizona. With this investment the company aims to expand its ambitions beyond rockets and Starklink satellite internet. According to a report by Reuters, the projects also include a proposed $50 billion campus in Arizona which would create 6,500 jobs but is facing opposition from local residents. In a statement on November 12, SpaceX said that it expects to spend more than $24 billion on a supercomputing facility at its Starbase site in Texas and approximately $50 billion on a second campus in Cochise County, Arizona.The proposed Arizona facility, which requires approval from Cochise County, is expected to generate around 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent positions. However, the project has drawn resistance from some residents. A petition carrying 2,400 signatures has urged local officials to reject the permit, with a public hearing scheduled for December.SpaceX said it is working with local electric cooperatives and claimed the project could reduce electricity bills for cooperative members by up to 20%. The company also said the facility would use dry cooling and would not rely on industrial groundwater use.SpaceX's $24 billion Texas AI computing campusThe second project is planned at SpaceX's Starbase site in Texas, where the company intends to invest more than $24 billion in a supercomputing facility and power infrastructure. A city notice published earlier this week outlined plans for a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility spread across approximately 444 acres. SpaceX said the Texas campus would generate its own electricity rather than draw power from the public grid.The project has already generated more than 3,000 construction jobs and is expected to support over 500 permanent jobs once operational. The Starbase City Commission is scheduled to consider a property tax abatement for the project on December 9.AI business becomes major revenue driver for SpaceXAs per the Reuters report, the planned investment from SpaceX comes at a time when AI computing is becoming a crucial and important part of SpaceX’s business. The AI segment of the company generated more than half of its revenue in the third quarter, this clearly highlights its increasing focus beyond rocket launches and satellite internet services. The two campuses in which SpaceX is planning to invest is said to expand the computing infrastructure of the company as it continues to invest in AI capabilities along with its present space and communications businesses.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: This one single habit at night was linked to a 20 to 30 per cent higher rate of fatty liver disease and cirrhosis in a US study of nearly 200,000 adults followed for decades by Oregon researchers.
articles.summary: We do everything, from going to the gym and measuring our calories with every bite to avoiding junk food, and yet somehow we still end up dealing with
articles.body: We do everything, from going to the gym and measuring our calories with every bite to avoiding junk food, and yet somehow we still end up dealing with bloating, fatigue and other health concerns. But have we ever stopped to think about whether our everyday habits, particularly when it comes to eating, could be affecting our liver health?While most of us spend most of our time reading the labels and measuring the nutritional value of our food, we do think about what we are eating, but how about when we eat? Could that also affect how our body reacts to those highly nutritious items? According to a new study, that midnight craving might be doing you more harm than you probably think.We all have midnight cravings. A few snacks or even a small energy bar are enough for us, especially in this day and age when irregular eating schedules have become fairly common, particularly with demanding work routines and jobs. But our bodies have an internal biological clock, and the liver is no exception. It follows a daily rhythm that helps regulate how the body processes nutrients, stores energy and manages fat. Eating at times when the body demands rest may interfere with these natural processes.To understand this connection, researchers from Oregon Health & Science University examined data from nearly 200,000 adults across long-running US health studies. Their findings suggested that people who regularly ate late at night had a higher rate of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), commonly known as fatty liver disease, as well as cirrhosis.Why the timing of your meals may matter as much as what you eatAs stated, our body works on a biological clock, which is known as the circadian rhythm, a natural 24-hour clock that helps the body regulate sleep and metabolism. And the liver is no exception. Moreover, our liver is one of the busiest organs in our body. Apart from filtering harmful substances, it also plays an important role in breaking down nutrients, regulating blood sugar and storing energy.When we eat late at night, we may be asking the body to process food at a time when it is naturally preparing for rest. The liver's metabolic activity changes throughout the day, and eating against these natural rhythms may affect how it handles fats and glucose. This is one possible explanation researchers are exploring to understand why late-night eating could be associated with a higher risk of liver disease.What did the researchers say?The findings are quite striking. Our liver does not work in the same way throughout the day. Like several other organs, it follows an internal biological clock that regulates how it processes nutrients and manages energy. Eating late at night may interfere with this natural rhythm.The researchers found that people who reported eating late at night had a 36 per cent higher relative risk of developing metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), while their risk of cirrhosis was 28 per cent higher compared with those who did not report this habit.The study analysed data from 199,155 participants across three long-running health studies: the Nurses' Health Study, Nurses' Health Study II and the Health Professionals' Follow-Up Study. Participants were followed for a median of approximately 16 years. This gave researchers an opportunity to examine the relationship between eating habits and liver health over a longer period.Can changing your meal timings make a difference?You do not necessarily have to give up your favourite midnight snacks or become overly conscious of every meal. But paying attention to when you eat could be a useful step towards better metabolic health. Researchers suggest that finishing your meals a few hours before bedtime and maintaining a more regular eating schedule may help your body work in sync with its natural biological clock.This does not mean that an occasional late-night meal will put your liver at risk. What matters is the pattern of your everyday habits. While more research is being done to understand the relationship between meal timings and liver disease more thoroughly, the findings offer an interesting reminder that eating well is not just about what goes on your plate, but also when you choose to eat it.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: For more than 20 years, Jim and Laura Currie burned and replanted their Mississippi land to bring back longleaf pine for gopher tortoises; now nearly 500 critically endangered dusky gopher frogs have been released there
articles.summary: Sometimes, giving wildlife a chance to survive begins with something as simple as opening up your own land to nature.
articles.body: Sometimes, giving wildlife a chance to survive begins with something as simple as opening up your own land to nature. For Jim and Laura Currie, a couple in Mississippi, it was just that. In more than two decades of working with biologists to restore their privately owned land, they have now helped create a home for an increasingly rare animal. The Mississippi gopher frog is listed as Endangered under the US Endangered Species Act and Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Nearly 500 dusky gopher frogs have been released on their property to help protect this rare amphibian in the United States.According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the release took place in June 2026 at Woodland Cottage, the Curries' property in Hancock County, Mississippi, as reported on July 29, 2026. The frogs were bred in captivity by the Memphis Zoo before being released into ponds across the restored land. The event was made possible through a collaboration involving the USFWS, the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks, the Memphis Zoo, Wildlife Mississippi and the couple themselves.A rare frog The dusky gopher frog (Lithobates sevosus), also known as the Mississippi gopher frog, is a rare amphibian native to the southeastern United States. Its historical range included parts of Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, but habitat loss and environmental changes have caused its population to decline dramatically.Unlike frogs that spend much of their lives around water, dusky gopher frogs spend much of their time underground, seeking shelter in burrows. One animal that provides these shelters is the gopher tortoise, whose burrows offer protection to several other species. The tortoise is considered a keystone species because its digging creates habitats that help support the wider community of wildlife.According to the USFWS, gopher tortoise burrows are used by more than 300 other species, including dusky gopher frogs. This relationship makes the restoration of suitable tortoise habitat particularly important, as the benefits extend well beyond the animal that originally occupied the land.The frogs also have specific breeding requirements. They depend on temporary wetlands and ponds, where females lay their eggs. These breeding sites need suitable vegetation and conditions that allow eggs and tadpoles to develop without being exposed to large predatory fish. The surrounding upland habitat is equally important because the frogs spend much of their time away from the water.Two decades of bringing back the longleaf pineThe Curries' conservation efforts began more than 20 years ago, when they started working with organisations including the USFWS Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program, Wildlife Mississippi and the US Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service.A major part of this work involved restoring the longleaf pine ecosystem, which had suffered considerable losses over the years because of land-use changes, deforestation and the suppression of natural fires.The Curries did not simply plant trees, but worked to bring back previously grazed and clear-cut areas by replanting longleaf pines and restoring grasses and flowering plants.Although deliberately setting fire to land might sound counterproductive when trying to restore a forest, fire is an important part of the natural longleaf pine ecosystem. Periodic, controlled burning helps maintain the open conditions and diverse ground vegetation that many native species depend on.Nearly 500 captive-bred frogs were released into ponds at Woodland Cottage in June 2026. This release has highlighted the conservation effort, but it is only the beginning.Establishing a population requires continued monitoring to understand whether the frogs survive, reproduce and gradually establish themselves in their new surroundings. The USFWS describes the release as an important milestone in a much larger recovery effort involving habitat restoration, captive breeding and cooperation between conservation organisations and private landowners.The Curries' property has given the frog a second chance at life, helping protect a rare amphibian and providing it with a home. A 20-year-long effort not only made this release possible but also helped restore an ecosystem that other wildlife can benefit from.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid in 2022; Europe's Hera probe has now reached the impact site to measure how successfully humanity can deflect a space rock
articles.summary: Humanity's first attempt to deliberately change the motion of an asteroid has entered a crucial new phase, with a European spacecraft reaching the site of
articles.body: Humanity's first attempt to deliberately change the motion of an asteroid has entered a crucial new phase, with a European spacecraft reaching the site of NASA's historic collision to investigate what happened beneath the debris. According to the Associated Press, the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has begun close inspections of the Didymos asteroid system and its smaller moonlet Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck in September 2022 as part of a planetary defence experiment. The spacecraft is currently observing the pair from approximately 25 to 30 kilometres away, gathering data that could help scientists determine whether deliberately crashing spacecraft into threatening asteroids can become a reliable way to protect Earth.The mission follows NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), which made history on September 26, 2022, when a spacecraft deliberately slammed into Dimorphos at approximately 22,000 km per hour. The collision was designed to test whether the force of a spacecraft hitting an asteroid could alter its movement, potentially providing humanity with a way to redirect space rocks that might otherwise collide with Earth.What happened when NASA deliberately hit an asteroid?Dimorphos is approximately 151 metres wide and orbits a much larger asteroid called Didymos, which measures around 780 metres in diameter. The two form a binary asteroid system, meaning the smaller object revolves around the larger one. Scientists selected the pair because their orbital relationship made it possible to measure the effects of the collision without having to send another spacecraft to observe the impact.NASA's DART spacecraft, weighing approximately 580 kg at the time of impact, was directed towards Dimorphos on September 26, 2022. Travelling at approximately 6.1 kilometres per second, it struck the asteroid in what became the first full-scale demonstration of a kinetic impactor being used to change the motion of a celestial object. The results exceeded the mission's initial expectations. Before the collision, Dimorphos took approximately 11 hours and 55 minutes to complete one orbit around Didymos. Following the impact, observations from telescopes on Earth confirmed that its orbital period had shortened by approximately 33 minutes.NASA initially reported a 32-minute change in October 2022, before subsequent measurements established a more precise reduction of 33 minutes, with an uncertainty of approximately one minute. The agency had defined a change of at least 73 seconds as the minimum threshold for mission success.The collision also produced a spectacular cloud of debris. Material thrown off Dimorphos extended more than 10,000 kilometres into space, while observations identified 37 metre-sized boulders that had been displaced from the asteroid. The material ejected during the collision is particularly important because it appears to have amplified the force of the spacecraft's impact.Why has Europe sent another spacecraft to the asteroid?Although DART successfully changed Dimorphos' orbit, the experiment left scientists with several unanswered questions. They know the collision altered the asteroid's movement, but understanding exactly how the impact changed its physical structure is essential before the technique can be used in a real planetary emergency.This is where ESA's Hera mission comes in. Launched in October 2024, the spacecraft has travelled through deep space to reach the Didymos system in November 2026. Its primary objective is to conduct a detailed investigation of the aftermath of the DART collision, measuring the asteroid's mass, composition, internal structure and the physical consequences of the impact.According to ESA's November 11 update, Hera has entered an early characterisation phase, maintaining a distance of approximately 25 to 30 kilometres from the asteroid pair. It is using this stage to collect broader observations of the two objects and determine how Dimorphos looks after being struck by NASA's spacecraft.The spacecraft is expected to move closer, to approximately 20 kilometres, as it enters its more detailed investigation phase in December. Scientists will examine whether DART created a distinct crater or dramatically reshaped the asteroid's surface. They also want to understand how much material was thrown into space and how the asteroid's internal structure influenced the impact.Hera's observations are particularly important for calculating what scientists call the momentum enhancement factor, or beta. It measures how effectively an impact transfers momentum to an asteroid, including the additional push produced when material is blasted away from its surface. A spacecraft does not simply transfer its own momentum to the target; the ejected debris can provide an additional force in the opposite direction.The mission will also deploy two smaller spacecraft, called CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani. These miniature probes will conduct closer investigations of the asteroid pair. Juventas is equipped with radar technology to investigate Dimorphos' internal structure, while Milani will study its surface composition and dust environment. The probes are also expected to approach and potentially land on Dimorphos after completing their observations.Could this experiment save Earth from an asteroid collision?The wider objective of the DART-Hera partnership is to establish whether the kinetic impact method can become a dependable planetary defence strategy. Scientists believe that if an asteroid heading towards Earth is detected sufficiently early, a spacecraft could potentially be sent to collide with it and gradually alter its trajectory.Even a relatively small change in an asteroid's movement could become significant over time, provided the intervention happens early enough. However, the success of such an operation would depend on several factors, including the asteroid's size, mass, composition, internal structure and the amount of time available before a potential collision.NASA has also reported that DART's impact slightly changed the orbit of the entire Didymos system around the Sun, in addition to changing Dimorphos' movement around its larger companion. Research published in March 2026 found that the system's roughly 770-day orbit around the Sun had changed by a fraction of a second, offering further evidence that a kinetic impact can influence an asteroid's trajectory.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: NASA has opened a $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge for US high school and college teams to solve problems like power, habitats and astronaut safety on the moon, and registration runs until 25 January
articles.summary: NASA has now invited students from across America to help tackle problems around a long-term lunar base through its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge.
articles.body: NASA has now invited students from across America to help tackle problems around a long-term lunar base through its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge. It was announced on November 8, 2026. The competition invites students from eligible US high schools and post-secondary institutions to develop innovative ideas for a future lunar base. This base shall provide astronauts a place where they could live, work and explore for extended periods. Registration is open until January 25, 2027, giving aspiring engineers, designers and problem-solvers a chance to contribute ideas to NASA's next chapter in space exploration.The announcement is more than an invitation to build impressive models. It is an opportunity to think about the practical realities of imagining life on the Moon. As NASA explains in its official announcement, students will help explore technologies needed to establish a sustained human presence near the lunar South Pole.Six problems standing between the Moon and a human homeA lunar base needs far more than a place to sleep and a window with a spectacular view of Earth. Every essential service must be designed to operate in an unforgiving environment, often with limited resources and minimal human intervention.NASA's competition therefore focuses on six areas, each addressing a different piece of the lunar-living puzzle.1. Power generation and storageElectricity is the backbone of a lunar settlement. A lunar base will have to operate communications equipment, heating systems, life-support machinery and other scientific instruments. Due to the Moon's unique rotation cycle there are periods when it stays in the dark. This requires solutions regarding electricity generation, storage and distribution when sunlight is unavailable.2. Habitat constructionAs attractive as it sounds, habitat construction on the Moon has challenges that seem unthinkable on Earth. After all, how do you build a shelter in a world where transporting every kilogram of material from Earth is expensive? Students can explore ways to construct durable structures using lunar soil, known as regolith, alongside robotic construction and other innovative techniques. The goal is to make habitats that can protect astronauts without depending entirely on supplies shipped from home.3. Life-support systemsOn Earth, air and water are things we rarely think about until something goes wrong. But, beyond that, the unavailability makes them more valuable than a Kohinoor. Students need to focus on building concepts that could address oxygen supply, water processing, waste management and the maintenance of a stable living environment.4. Surface mobilityAstronauts and robots living on the lunar base will need to move across the Moon's dusty, uneven terrain. Mobility will be required to transport equipment, conduct experiments and explore the surrounding landscape. Solutions around better rovers and autonomous vehicles could make these journeys safer and more efficient.5. Communication networksA settlement on the Moon needs reliable ways to exchange information not just between astronauts but also between vehicles, equipment and other facilities. Thus, students are encouraged to propose communication networks that remain reliable despite the Moon's harsh operating conditions.6. Astronaut safetyLunar dust can damage equipment, radiation in space poses health risks, and tiny micrometeorites can threaten exposed structures. Ideas involving protective materials, hazard monitoring, emergency procedures and safer equipment could help reduce those dangers.The competition's official rules and eligibility guide outline these six categories and the environmental conditions teams must consider.The Moon is not an easy place to improviseThe challenge is not just building a home, it is to sustain it on the Moon where conditions are drastically different from those on Earth. According to the competition's technical guidelines, teams should account for extreme temperature swings, radiation, abrasive dust, low gravity and the challenges of operating in a vacuum.Their designs should also be lightweight, energy-efficient and reliable, with limited dependence on supplies from Earth. A brilliant habitat concept, for instance, will not be particularly useful if it requires constant repairs by astronauts or materials that cannot realistically reach the lunar surface.Who can participate, and how does it work?The competition is designed for eligible student teams in the United States, with separate divisions for high school and post-secondary students. Teams must have two to five student members along with an adult coach. Participants must meet the competition's institutional and individual eligibility requirements, so interested students should read the official rules before registering.The challenge follows multiple phases, taking teams from developing a concept to submitting more detailed proposals. Students can choose one of the above mentioned six technical categories and work on a solution suited to their interests, whether that means designing an energy-storage system, exploring lunar construction materials or developing technology to protect astronauts. The competition is intended to help participants build practical skills, work collaboratively and explore potential careers in the space industry.Registration takes place through NASA's STEM Gateway, and the Moon Base Student Challenge website provides the competition's rules, guidance and updates. The registration deadline is January 25, 2027.The next breakthrough in space technology might not begin in a high-security research laboratory. It might start with a group of students around a classroom table, a rough sketch of a habitat and a deceptively simple question: What would it take to call the Moon home?Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Road construction in Kerala threatened thousands of rare orchids growing on trees, so researchers moved 27,324 plants to new sites; two years later, more than 19,500 had survived, and some were flowering
articles.summary: Many development projects across the world have, over the years, put the habitats of plants and wildlife at risk.
articles.body: Many development projects across the world have, over the years, put the habitats of plants and wildlife at risk. But when researchers in Kerala were faced with the possibility of thousands of orchids losing the trees they called home to road-widening projects, they began asking a rather unusual question: could these plants be relocated to a new habitat? Would they continue to grow, flower and reproduce even after being moved somewhere new? In an effort to give the orchids another chance at survival, scientists set out to find them a new home, with plenty of questions about whether they would adapt to their unfamiliar surroundings.A study published in the Plants journal on October 15, 2026, looked at whether thousands of orchid plants could be saved from destruction through a rescue relocation effort. The research was carried out by Mithun Venugopal, Pradeep N. Sukumaran and Viswambharan Sarasan, with researchers from the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode and the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK.Why were the orchids at risk?Orchids are often associated with colourful flowers and ornamental gardens, but there is much more to this plant family than meets the eye. Some species grow on other plants, particularly trees, and are known as epiphytic orchids. Unlike parasitic plants, they do not take nutrients from their hosts. Instead, the trees provide them with a surface on which to grow, while their roots absorb moisture from their surroundings. This reliance on trees for growth, however, can make them vulnerable when their host trees are removed. A tree that is felled may take an entire community of orchids with it, including plants that have been growing there for years.The Western Ghats, which extend through the state of Kerala, provide a distinctive landscape. Their rainfall and climatic conditions offer habitats for numerous species, many of which have a limited distribution. However, with road development and widening projects bringing changes to the landscape, roadside trees have increasingly become vulnerable to removal.Giving the orchids another place to growThe researchers rescued 27,324 mature orchids, belonging to 21 species, from trees that had already been felled or were scheduled to be removed during road-widening work. These plants were subsequently relocated to three sites in Kozhikode: Sarovaram Bio Park, Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. These species have particular growing requirements, and simply attaching them to another tree does not guarantee that they will survive. The type of host tree, the amount of moisture available, sunlight and the surrounding environment can all influence how well they establish themselves.The three locations selected for the rescued orchids also offered rather different conditions. Sarovaram Bio Park is an urban wetland with mangrove cover, Malabar Botanical Garden has a mixture of shaded and marshy areas, while Kappad Beach is an exposed coastal landscape, where plants face stronger winds, sunlight and air laden with salt.More than 19,500 orchids survivedThe findings, assessed over a period of 12 to 24 months, were encouraging. Of the 27,324 orchids relocated, 19,511 survived, accounting for 71.4% of the plants. More interestingly, the effort did not merely keep them alive. Researchers found that 5,224 of the surviving orchids had flowered, while 1,934 went on to produce seed capsules.The results, however, varied across the three sites. Sarovaram Bio Park recorded the highest survival rate, with 87.7% of the relocated orchids surviving there. At Malabar Botanical Garden, the survival rate stood at 47.3%, while Kappad Beach recorded 28.7%.The researchers also relocated 6,126 plants belonging to 12 regionally endemic species, of which 3,368 survived. This meant that approximately 55% of these orchids had managed to establish themselves in their new surroundings. Some of these species are associated with cooler, hilly and mist-covered habitats, making their relocation to sites closer to sea level particularly challenging.Taking conservation beyond the plants themselvesThere was another aspect to the project that extended beyond relocating the orchids. Researchers also wanted visitors to become more familiar with the plants growing around them, particularly species that might otherwise go unnoticed. Therefore, at Sarovaram Bio Park, 10 selected orchid species were provided with QR-code labels, allowing visitors to scan them and learn more about the plants. Over two years, these labels generated 126,251 scans. To their surprise, even orchids with smaller and far less conspicuous flowers gained traction.The researchers also found that root growth was an important indicator of how well the relocated orchids were performing. However, they cautioned that producing flowers and seed capsules does not necessarily mean that a new population will be able to sustain itself. Only longer-term monitoring can help researchers understand whether the plants can reproduce successfully and establish self-sustaining populations. But ultimately, the study has provided insight into the possibilities of exploring more dynamic approaches to nature conservation.

articles.title: Underwater archaeologists exploring Lake Superior documented an 1880s flooded silver mine and found two rail cars lost in a 2008 derailment; a remote submersible reached nearly 40 metres below the surface
articles.summary: A place where different periods of history coalesce, might perhaps be under water, where time is still unmoving.
articles.body: A place where different periods of history coalesce, might perhaps be under water, where time is still unmoving. Lake Superior, in North America, beneath its blue depths, has surprised researchers with findings that date back to the mining industry of the 1880s, but also to the evidence from a railway derailment in 2008.According to a report by TimminsToday, underwater archaeologists from Parks Canada explored several historical sites in Lake Superior during the summer, including the remains of an old silver mine and two railway cars that had plunged into the lake following a train derailment in 2008. The investigations have been a part of the agency's continuing effort to document archaeological resources underwater in the Lake Superior National Marine Conservation Area. What makes the exploration particularly interesting is that researchers were not only looking at shipwrecks, but also at industrial structures and objects that tell us about the ways people once worked and travelled around the region.Exploring the remains of a historic silver mineOne of the sites examined by the underwater archaeology team was the Silver Islet mine, an offshore silver mining operation that functioned during the 1870s and continued into the mid-1880s. Located beneath the waters of Lake Superior, the mine was once considered the world's richest silver mine, but what made it even more unusual was that it wa an offshore mine.Mining beneath a lake was no ordinary undertaking. The operatiosn depended on protective structures and pumps which prevent water from entering the shafts. Breakwaters were constructed around the site to protect it from the lake, while pumps had to operate continuously to keep the underground workings from flooding.According to Ontario Parks, in an article dated January 25, 2022, the Silver Islet mine shaft is hundreds of metres deep into the lake. During the recent investigation, the underwater archaeologists had focused on documenting what remained of the original breakwater and the mine shafts. However, exploring the interior was not straightforward. There was considerable debris obstructing the way, which prevented divers from travelling very far inside the mine. Instead, the team used a remotely operated submersible vehicle to investigate the deeper sections, reaching nearly 40 metres below the surface.The vehicle helped researchers document the shaft structures and ladders that connected on different levels of the mine. Rather than simply recording the location of an abandoned mine, the team was able to examine surviving structures that reveal something about the way workers once moved through the site.Although the Silver Islet mine is not technically within the boundaries of the Lake Superior National Marine Conservation Area, it remains privately owned, the team received permission to study it. Its historical significance made it an important site to document, particularly because it forms part of the local history of the region.Two railway cars that remained underwater since 2008The investigation also took the archaeologists to another location along Lake Superior's North Shore, near Rossport. This time, the focus was not a mining operation but two railway cars that had plunged into the lake during a train derailment in 2008. The cars were never recovered and had remained underwater since the incident.According to TimminsToday, Parks Canada's underwater archaeology team had received information about the submerged railway cars from people who had repeatedly brought the incident to their attention. This led the researchers to then examine the location and try to identify the rail cars. The investigation team was interested in more than simply confirming the railway cars were still there, they also hoped to understand what they had been carrying when they entered the water. So, finally, their examination suggested that one car contained some type of paper, allowing them to determine the specificities of what they had discovered.Documenting what lies beneath Lake SuperiorThe work was carried out by Parks Canada's 12-member underwater archaeology unit, which consists of diving specialists who examined the submerged landscapes, such as shipwrecks and other archaeological sites. The team also works to gather information that can help Parks Canada develop future interpretation programmes and make these sites better understood by the public.The Lake Superior National Marine Conservation Area itself covers more than 10,000 square kilometres, extending across a substantial portion of the Canadian side of the lake. It includes waters stretching from the Sibley Peninsula towards the Slate Islands and the marine border between Canada and the United States. With such a vast area to investigate, documenting every underwater site is a considerable undertaking.As Charles Dagneau, acting manager of Parks Canada's underwater archaeology team, explained to TimminsToday, the work is also dependent on the lake and its weather conditions. Even when researchers know where to look, reaching and documenting a particular site is not always possible. The natural world, or rather in this case, the lake can be a vessel, a repository of human history, where the same site can preserve remains of a 19th century mining operation and also hold traces of an unprecedented accident from the 21st century.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: A tiger's urine and scat may reveal more than its presence; researchers distinguished tigers from leopards with 79% and 75% accuracy, suggesting a non-invasive tool for monitoring big cats
articles.summary: The forests are ruled by the cat families. They are feral, ferocious and far too similar, so spotting them is never an easy task.
articles.body: The forests are ruled by the cat families. They are feral, ferocious and far too similar, so spotting them is never an easy task. For researchers studying big cats, this means looking into the traces they leave behind. If you have ever been on a safari and your guide has pointed towards their paw prints, scratch marks or droppings, you know that they are onto something and so are the researchers. While these signs have long helped researchers understand which animal might have passed through an area, it can leave behind traces of its presence without ever appearing in front of a camera or a person. But did you know that even the odour of a tiger's urine or scat could offer clues about the animal, including the species it belongs to and possibly aspects of its age, sex and reproductive health?A study published in the Journal of Chemical Ecology on May 29, 2026, explored chemical compounds released by tiger and leopard urine and feces, leading researchers to distinguish between the two species and question the veracity with which they can be differentiated.The study, titled Non-Invasive Sampling of Odours from Tiger (Panthera tigris) and Leopard (Panthera pardus) for Wildlife Conservation, was conducted by researchers from the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Ahmedabad University and the Danish Academy of Technical Sciences.The researchers were at first interested in volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which are chemical compounds that evaporate and are released into the air. These compounds can carry information about an animal's physiological appearance and can play a role in how anials communicate amongst themselves . By examining the chemical composition of urine and faeces, researchers, had hoped to identify patterns that could help distinguish one species from another, whilst also seeing what other infromation could be gathered about the indivudal species.To investigate this, the team collected urine and scat samples from captive Bengal tigers and Indian leopards whose ages and sexes were known. They also collected urine samples from identified wild Bengal tigers, for which information about age, sex and reproductive status was available. This allowed them to examine whether the chemical signatures found in the samples corresponded with characteristics that were already known about the animals.Analysing the chemical cluesCollecting the samples was only one part of the process. The researchers used a technique called headspace solid-phase field sampling to capture the volatile compounds released by the urine and faeces. These compounds were then analysed using thermal desorption-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.The team then used a machine-learning technique, called Random Forest, to monitor the chemical patterns and identify compounds that could serve as possible indicators of species, age, sex and reproductive state.R researchers were able to classify tigers and leopards with an accuracy of approximately 79% using urine samples and 75% using scat samples. The study also revealed that these chemical markers could offer clues about age and sex, although the veracity varied depending on the group being examined. As, Urine samples provided stronger classification results for females and younger individuals, while older animals and males were more difficult to distinguish. Scat samples, meanwhile, performed better across different groups.Beyond identifying the speciesPerhaps one of the more interesting aspects of the research is the possibility that animal odours could reveal information beyond species identification. The researchers also identified potential chemical markers associated with reproductive status in tigers. One of the findings concerned nonanol, a compound found in higher abundance in urine samples from pregnant and lactating female tigers than in non-reproductive females. The team also observed elevated levels of another compound, dimethyl tetrasulphide, in the scat of a captive tiger being treated for epilepsy. However, this finding came from an individual animal and would require further investigation before the compound could be considered a reliable indicator of the condition.While these findings are only in their preliminary phase, they do open up an interesting possibility for wildlife monitoring. Details about an animals’s reproductive state for instance could help understand the population and breeding patterns without actually having to physically examine the animal.Monitoring big cats in their natural habitats often involves techniques such as camera trapping and genetic sampling. While these methods can help researchers estimate population numbers, density and, in some cases, identify individual animals, they may not always provide information about their physiological condition. Analysing chemical signatures could potentially add another layer to this understanding.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
articles.summary: SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but th...
articles.body:
SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.

It's the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk's company missed out on a double catch.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.

SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising.

"Well, that certainly isn't the news that we had hoped to hear for today," observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.

This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated.

The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is "how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000," SpaceX's Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida's Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX's smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Falcon rockets "are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we're going to catch both the first stage and second stage," Dontchev said ahead of Friday's launch.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk's Starship or Bezos' Blue Moon.

During next summer's Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.

"We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

articles.title: Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
articles.summary: As Jensen Huang’s sex scandal thrusts Nvidia into the limelight, environmental advocates are pressuring Nvidia to clean up its dirty supply chain.
articles.body: Under cofounder Jensen Huang, Nvidia has become the engine for the AI boom — and one of the tech industry’s biggest environmental liabilities. Its sought-after chips have triggered a new wave of water- and chemical-intensive factories, drained power grids from inside massive data centers, and set the stage for a looming e-waste problem. Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia clashed with environmental groups seeking to hold the company accountable for its so-called “hidden” emissions. Huang has talked up the idea of using AI to fight climate change while his company’s supply chain emissions ballooned. Nvidia’s investments, meanwhile, have supported the buildout of data centers that have sparked intense backlash for both their local and global impact. Now, after the CEO’s shocking resignation amid a sprawling sex-and-espionage scandal, advocates are urging Nvidia to turn the page. “Jensen Huang has failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy, to slow down the unchecked expansion of data centres or to prevent its chips from being deployed in unethical applications like automated warfare,” Avex Li, Greenpeace East Asia’s project lead for AI supply chain campaign, said in a press release Thursday. The organization is now pushing interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing by investing in renewable energy, as well as ensuring its technology is used in a way that “respects human rights.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge. Huang has projected optimism about how AI can boost the adoption of renewable energy, even as the planet-heating emissions of tech companies — including his own — have grown in the generative AI era. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into A.I. It is the best opportunity we have to get there,” Huang said in a September episode of The Ezra Klein Show, arguing that electricity demand for AI is leading companies to buy more sustainable energy. In the same interview, however, he admitted data centers will rely on more fossil fuels in the near term, and that building up the infrastructure for AI will likely result in “an enormous amount of pain and suffering.” He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.” Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. It’s an increase of about 9.4 million metric tons of planet-heating pollution, roughly equivalent to the emissions from nearly 25 gas plants over a year. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report. Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi. Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture. Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases. Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. When Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang’s speech at Nvidia GTC in Berlin last month, he responded onstage by saying, “I’ll talk to you guys later … All important issues, but let me get through my keynote.” In the Thursday press release, Greenpeace says Nvidia has yet to meet with Greenpeace despite the organization’s attempts to “seek dialogue” with the company over the past two years. “One of Huang’s defining legacies is inflating a speculative AI bubble, pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure with little regard for the real-world consequences inflicted on local communities and the climate,” Katrin Wu, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in an email to The Verge. “Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.” Beyond Nvidia’s day-to-day operations, Huang threw his weight around as the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies — chumming it up with President Donald Trump and lobbying for the US to allow sales of its powerful chips to China. The company’s influence on the global economy extended beyond chips as it invested in data centers stocking its GPUs. And with electricity supply often the thorniest bottleneck to building more and bigger data centers, Nvidia’s long tendrils reached into the energy sector as well. NVentures, the company’s venture capital arm, has funded battery recycling company Redwood Materials and startups developing AI tools to optimize power grids and make data centers more responsive to fluctuations in energy demand. Nvidia joined one of those startups, Emerald AI, along with Google to cofound the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) in September. The alliance advocates for strategies that tech companies promote as ways to keep data centers from overwhelming power grids or raising utility bills for other customers, including generating power on-site and making “flexible” facilities that can pause operations during times of peak energy demand. Notably, some environmental groups argue that those measures might just help data centers come online faster without fully insulating households from the impact that rising electricity demand has on their air quality or utility bills. Whether Nvidia’s environmental footprint shrinks or expands from here will depend on whoever steps in to fill Huang’s shoes. Over the years, Greenpeace and other environmental groups have pointed out that despite having an outsize impact on the environment, Nvidia doesn’t necessarily come under the same public scrutiny as more consumer-facing brands like Apple or Google. Huang’s exploits have thrust the company into a new kind of spotlight, however, just as data centers increasingly face backlash from nearby communities. Nvidia won’t be able to hide from the glare.

articles.title: Exclusive: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Drogue is harvesting heat from the ocean to power data centers on floating vessels. The first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, in less than two years.
articles.body:
Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever.

A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers.

Drogue , which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now.

The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.”

Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors.

In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms.

To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious.

After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said.

As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it.

The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s.

Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said.

To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then released, and dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats.

The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said.

To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said.

There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said.

Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean.

In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers : find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.
