articles.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceX to attempt double catch of Starship rocket
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s company will try to grab both parts of the rocket for the first time.
articles.body:
SpaceX will attempt to catch both parts of its huge Starship rocket after it launches on its next test flight on Friday.

Elon Musk's company will use the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower to grab the rocket parts mid-air as they return to Earth.

If successful, this will be the first full recovery of a rocket that's been to space, paving the way for making Starship reusable so it can fly repeatedly.

Nasa will be closely watching the flight: the SpaceX rocket is set to play a vital part in its Artemis programme, which will see astronauts land on the Moon.

The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.

After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.

The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.

Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.

SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.

If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.

In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.

Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.

But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society.

"A successful double catch would be visually spectacular, but full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.

"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."

What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?

Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test

After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.

The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.

SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.

Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.

This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.

Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.

Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title: Most people dislike coffee at first and learn to love it, and scientists now say the reason may be a slow dopamine signal from the gut that teaches the brain to like flavours linked with calories, even bitter ones
articles.summary: Do you remember your first sip of coffee? The one that almost made you throw up? And look at you now.
articles.body: Do you remember your first sip of coffee? The one that almost made you throw up? And look at you now. A good cup of coffee is probably the first thing your hand reaches for every morning. But how is it that something that initially tastes so bitter and unpleasant eventually becomes something you look forward to?We mostly think that whatever we like or dislike is because of the taste. But you too must have noticed that many foods you couldn't even touch a few years ago have now become your favourites. So, if the food hasn't changed, what has? Scientists might have found something, and the answer could be linked to your gut and brain rather than just your taste buds.According to a study published in the journal Nature, titled "The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning", researchers have identified a gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that may help explain how we learn to enjoy flavours associated with calories, even bitter ones. The study suggests that our food preferences may not be determined by taste alone. In fact, our gut may have a much bigger role to play in deciding what we eventually enjoy eating. When we consume food, the nutrients it provides send signals from the gut to the brain, where dopamine, a chemical associated with reward and motivation, helps reinforce the connection between a particular flavour and the nutritional benefits that follow.This could explain why some foods that we initially find unpleasant gradually become part of our everyday diet. But how exactly does this communication between the gut and brain work, and what did the researchers discover?How the gut teaches the brain to like certain foodsThe process we are looking at is known as flavour-nutrient learning. In simple terms, the brain learns to associate a particular taste with the nutritional benefits that follow. So, even if a flavour initially seems unpleasant, the nutritional reward associated with it can gradually make us more likely to enjoy it.So, when we eat something, the gut sends signals about the nutrients entering our body, helping the brain understand the nutritional value of what we have consumed. Researchers found that these signals trigger a slow release of dopamine in a region of the brain associated with learning and reward.In their experiments, the researchers found that this dopamine activity was linked to the anterior basolateral amygdala, a region involved in learning and assigning value to experiences. They studied how mice responded to different flavours paired with nutritional rewards. When the gut-to-brain dopamine pathway was disrupted, the mice struggled to develop preferences for flavours associated with nutrients. However, stimulating the pathway could encourage them to develop such preferences.But how does a chemical influence what food we like?The role of dopamine in developing food preferencesDopamine is often called the feel-good chemical, but its role goes beyond simply making us feel happy. It is closely involved in how we learn from rewarding experiences and develop preferences. In this study, researchers found that the gut-triggered dopamine signal was not an instant response but a slow and sustained one. This is important because it allows the brain to connect the taste of food with the nutritional reward that follows.To understand this better, the researchers examined what happened when this dopamine pathway was switched off or artificially activated in mice. When the pathway was disrupted, the animals struggled to develop a preference for flavours associated with nutrients. On the other hand, activating it could encourage them to prefer certain flavours, even without receiving the corresponding nutritional reward. This suggests that dopamine does not simply make food taste better; it helps the brain learn which flavours are worth returning to.Why we learn to enjoy bitter foods like coffeeThis brings us back to our morning cup of coffee. Unlike sweet foods, which we often enjoy from the very first bite, bitter flavours can take some getting used to. Coffee, dark chocolate and certain vegetables are common examples. We may initially find their taste unpleasant, but repeated exposure and the nutritional rewards associated with food can gradually influence our preferences.The researchers' findings offer a possible explanation for this process. The gut-to-brain dopamine pathway helps the brain learn to associate flavours with the calories and nutrients they provide. This means that our liking for certain foods may develop through more than just repeated exposure or changes in our taste perception. However, the study does not establish that this pathway is directly responsible for humans acquiring a taste for coffee. Rather, it offers a possible biological explanation for how food preferences develop over time.And perhaps that's what it shows: love grows. Coffee was never meant to be love at first sip. It is something that grows on you, little by little and sip by sip.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Physicists Find a Mathematical Limit to Making Time Run Backward
articles.summary: Why does it only go one way?
articles.body:
Our experience of time seems uniform and unidirectional, but relativity allows it to be a bit more loosey-goosey than you might expect.

For example, in a strong gravitational field, time runs more slowly compared to time farther away – as though gravity itself were dragging it out.

Likewise, if you travel fast enough, time will pass more slowly for you compared to someone who stays behind.

In these examples, time still only flows in one direction.

But looking beyond relativity, into the realm of quantum mechanics, another possibility emerges – one in which time might not merely slow down, but effectively run backward.

What happens when it does, though? A new mathematical exploration of this question has returned a surprising answer: The quantum environment itself imposes a limit on how far back time can effectively run.

For the simplest model explored by physicists Yakir Aharonov of Tel Aviv University and Avshalom C. Elitzur of the Israel Institute for Advanced Research, time could only effectively run backward for about a femtosecond – or one quadrillionth of a second.

Their work is detailed in a preprint uploaded to arXiv .

This isn't Aharonov's first time-reversal rodeo.

In 1990, he and his colleagues proposed a theoretical device called a quantum time-translation machine, which could exploit the strange properties of quantum mechanics to make a system behave as though time had sped up, stopped, or even run backward.

The idea hinges on a quirk of quantum mechanics called superposition, in which a system can exist in a combination of different possible states at once.

Imagine you have a clock in such a state of superposition, occupying two different positions in a gravitational field at once – with enough of a difference in gravitational strength to affect the rate at which time passes.

In one position, deeper in the gravitational field, time passes more slowly. In the other, farther away, time passes more quickly.

Quantum mechanics allows both possibilities to coexist. And when the two branches of the clock are brought back together, they can interfere with each other.

Here's where things get weird. By selecting a particular outcome of that interference – a process called post-selection – physicists can theoretically make the clock behave as though it has experienced an amount of time outside the range of either possibility.

That could mean more time than has passed for either branch. It could mean no time at all. Or it could mean a negative amount of time – as though the clock had been running backward.

Now, 36 years later, Aharonov and Elitzur have returned to the idea to investigate a particularly thorny question: How far could that negative time actually go?

Because the concept remains theoretical, rather than experimentally realized, the pair turned to mathematics to explore four slightly different configurations of the machine.

But before they could start, they had to answer a deceptively simple question.

Suppose you do manage to make time run backward. How in the heck do you prove it?

And this is where a little bit of atomic decay steals the floor.

When an atom absorbs energy, one of its electrons can jump to a higher energy level, putting the atom into what's known as an excited state.

But atoms are a little bit lazy – they tend to settle back to their unexcited state (relatable). Eventually, the electron can drop back to a lower energy level, releasing the excess energy as a photon. This process is called spontaneous emission, and under ordinary circumstances, it only goes one way.

So the researchers proposed starting with a collection of atoms that had already begun to decay, and seeing whether their theoretical machine could reverse the process.

Imagine you have 100 excited atoms. You wait until some of them have released their energy, leaving just 80 still excited.

Now suppose you put those 100 atoms through the theoretical time machine.

If you end up with more than 80 excited atoms, the machine has effectively reversed some of the decay that had already taken place.

Now, if time really did run backward, the emitted light would have to return to the atoms, restoring them to their excited states – which poses a new problem. The photons might already have traveled away, or been absorbed by something else.

To account for all of this, Aharonov and Elitzur imagined enclosing the atoms inside a completely sealed cell, along with the light they emitted and walls that could absorb it.

The entire cell would then pass through the theoretical machine, allowing the researchers to investigate whether the whole process could effectively be reversed.

And here's where a rather draconian barrier emerged.

Even inside a sealed cell, the atoms don't exist in isolation. As they emit light, they interact with the surrounding electromagnetic field, leaving traces of what has happened.

For the simplest version of the machine, reversing the decay depends on those interactions retaining the quantum coherence needed for the two possible histories to interfere.

But that window doesn't stay open for long.

In the researchers' optical example, it lasts around one femtosecond.

Beyond that, the environment has effectively retained too much information about the emission for the simplest two-branch machine to produce the desired reversal.

So the limit isn't imposed by time – it's imposed by the environment's memory of the light.

More elaborate versions of the machine could theoretically reverse longer intervals, but only by introducing vastly more quantum branches, with increasingly improbable chances of success.

But what, you are now no doubt asking, about the second law of thermodynamics? A salient point, sage reader, and one the researchers addressed directly.

According to the second law of thermodynamics, the total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease. Natural processes tend to move in one direction, from more ordered states to less ordered ones.

As Sir Arthur Eddington so succinctly put it, "If your theory is found to be against the Second law of thermodynamics I can give you no hope; there is nothing for it but to collapse in deepest humiliation."

But if time could run in reverse, wouldn't that violate the second law? Well, not necessarily.

The loophole lies in post-selection. The apparent reversal of time occurs only in a very small fraction of possible outcomes, carefully selected from all the others.

When all the outcomes are considered together, the system as a whole still obeys the second law of thermodynamics. Entropy hasn't magically started decreasing across the board.

So Aharonov and Elitzur's theoretical machine can produce something that looks like time running backward without overturning one of the most fundamental laws of physics – thus evading Eddington's threatened humiliation.

But why go to such extraordinary lengths to risk an eggy face?

Well, because the question isn't really whether we can build a machine that sends things backward through time. It's why time appears to move in only one direction in the first place.

Many of the fundamental equations of physics work just as well backward as forward. Yet the world we experience is full of processes that seem impossible to undo.

By identifying exactly where quantum time reversal breaks down, Aharonov and Elitzur's work could help physicists understand how the environment gives rise to the irreversible processes that define our experience of time.

"The arrow of time enters exactly where the machine stops," the researchers write .

The research is available on preprint server arXiv .

articles.body: SpaceX's attempt to recover both stages of its Starship rocket during a single mission was thwarted on Friday after the Super Heavy booster ended up in the Gulf, with the company saying it would not attempt to recover it due to a technical issue, as cited by AP.The launch was part of SpaceX's most ambitious Starship test yet, a 22-hour mission aimed at demonstrating the recovery of both the rocket's booster and upper stage. The company hopes to make the entire rocket reusable, a development that could significantly accelerate launch operations and support future missions to the Moon and Mars.If successful, the test would have marked the first time that every part of a rocket launched into orbit was recovered for reuse. SpaceX founder Elon Musk sees full reusability as key to achieving the rapid and frequent launch rates needed to build bases on the Moon and send humans to Mars.The previous test in September was the first Starship mission to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not attempt to recover either rocket stage.SpaceX plans to begin launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in the coming years. The company believes expanded launch infrastructure and full rocket reusability will be essential to scaling up its operations."How do you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 1,00,000," Dontchev said.Meanwhile, SpaceX's smaller Falcon rockets will continue to carry astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA from Cape Canaveral and launch Starlink satellites from California. Other satellites will also continue to use Falcon rockets for now, although Musk intends for Starship to eventually replace them."Falcon rockets are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we're going to catch both the first stage and second stage," Dontchev said.Nasa has committed billions of dollars to SpaceX to develop Starship as a lunar lander for its Artemis programme. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is another major contender for the contract. Nasa is expected to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing, the first crewed Moon landing in more than half a century, whether to use Musk's Starship or Bezos' Blue Moon lander.During the Artemis III mission, scheduled for next summer, astronauts will practise docking their spacecraft with both Blue Moon and Starship in orbit around Earth. articles.title: For nearly 300 years, visitors to Scotland’s Balquhidder churchyard have admired Rob Roy MacGregor’s gravestone, but 3D scans now suggest its first carvings were made about 1,000 years before he died
articles.summary: \"Far and near, through vale and hill, Are faces that attest the same, And kindle like a fire new stirr'd, At sound of Rob Roy's name\", wrote William
articles.body: "Far and near, through vale and hill,Are faces that attest the same,And kindle like a fire new stirr'd,At sound of Rob Roy's name", wrote William Wordsworth in the poem Rob Roy's Grave (1905), later to be used in an introduction of Sir Walter Scott's novel, Rob Roy set in year 1715.Some larger-than-life heroes have been indelibly etched into stories of valour through the ages. Among the stories of the Scottish Highlands, one tale that has reverberated through time is that of Rob Roy MacGregor. His gravestone, which has been admired and visited by people for nearly 300 years, is now believed to contain carvings that may predate his death by as much as a thousand years.The discovery was made through 3D imaging of the elaborate stone slab at Balquhidder Parish Church in Scotland, where a grave believed to belong to MacGregor is marked by an elaborately carved stone slab. The imaging drew attention to carvings that appear to belong to an early period of Christian history, suggesting the stone was reused and modified over several centuries before becoming associated with the Scottish outlaw.The Balquhidder Graveyard Claymore Project, committed to documenting and studying the historic carved stones found in the churchyard, has been working to locate and identify graveslabs using photogrammetry. This is a method of creating detailed three-dimensional models using photographs, allowing researchers to examine the surfaces of gravestones more closely, record carvings and identify details that may otherwise be difficult to distinguish.In a press release published on October 30, 2026, Elaine Black of the Balquhidder Graveyard Claymore Project described the discovery as a story spanning more than a thousand years. She also suggested that Rob Roy himself might have appreciated the unusual history of the stone had he been alive to see the findings.A gravestone with a much older historyRobert MacGregor, popularly known as Rob Roy, was a prominent figure in 17th- and 18th-century Scottish history. Often remembered as an outlaw and folk hero, his reputation grew considerably after the publication of The Highland Rogue, a fictionalised account of his life, in 1723. His story was later immortalised by Scottish novelist Sir Walter Scott in his 1817 novel Rob Roy, helping establish the image of the Highland figure in popular culture.When MacGregor died in 1734, he was buried at Balquhidder Parish Church, where an elaborately carved stone slab is believed to mark his resting place. However, archaeologists had already suspected that the stone was considerably older than the eighteenth century and had been reused for a later burial.According to Archaeology Magazine, in an article published on November 9, 2026, the recent 3D imaging revealed a cross-like carving near the top of the stone that appears to belong to the early medieval period. The design has been interpreted as possibly depicting a flabellum, a ceremonial fan that was once used during Catholic religious services. The unusual carving is accompanied by two smaller crosses on either side, adding to the possibility that the stone originally belonged to an early medieval religious setting.What the carvings revealThe identification of the possible flabellum is particularly interesting because it offers a clue about the person for whom the stone may initially have been created. A flabellum was a ceremonial object used in Catholic liturgy, and its depiction on a carved stone could suggest an association with the clergy. Researchers therefore believe that the slab may originally have been made for an important cleric connected to the early medieval church.Dr Kelly Kilpatrick, who identified the fan-like design during a recent site visit, also drew attention to the two smaller crosses positioned alongside it. These have been carved using a technique known as pocking and smoothing, which is characteristic of early Christian sculpture. The arrangement of three crosses is also a familiar feature of early medieval stonework, with the largest representing the cross on which Jesus Christ was crucified.However, the stone did not remain unchanged throughout its history. The carvings appear to have been added at different periods of time, with some of the more recognisable images belonging to a much later phase. These include a sword, a pair of tongs and what may be a scene depicting hunting or herding, which are believed to have been added sometime during the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries.There is also a carved figure that has been interpreted as a possible depiction of Rob Roy himself, shown with a kilt and shield. Interestingly, even this image may have been adapted from an older medieval carving, rather than being made specifically to represent MacGregor. This means that the slab could have undergone several rounds of modification before it was eventually placed over the grave believed to belong to him.The project has also been making these digital models available online, allowing people to become part of the exploration of the carvings and inscriptions. With the recently revealed archaeological evidence, the history of this gravestone now offers an insight into a past that was not previously understood, tracing a story that predates the very hero it has come to epitomise.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: SpaceX launches 15th Starship flight; aborts booster recovery maneuver
articles.summary: SpaceX launched the 15th uncrewed flight of its next-generation Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday.
articles.body: SpaceX launched the 15th uncrewed flight of its next-generation Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday. The company hopes the mission will be the first round-trip rocket voyage to orbit and then back to the very spot where it left Earth. If all goes as planned, Starship’s upper-stage vessel will re-enter the atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit. SpaceX planned to use a “chopstick”-arm technology to recover Starship’s lower-stage booster rocket shortly after the two parts of the spacecraft separate within minutes of the launch. That maneuver was aborted shortly after the launch, according to a video livestream provided by the company. It wasn’t immediately clear why that process was not completed. The booster splashed down in the ocean Gulf of Mexico instead. Bringing the top portion of the spacecraft safely intact to the platform where it was launched to orbit would mark a breakthrough in SpaceX founder Elon Musk’s ambition to produce a fully reusable rocket system. The combined vehicle, consisting of the main Starship cargo-and-crew vessel perched atop its Super Heavy booster rocket and standing 40 stories high, roared off its launch pad Friday evening from SpaceX’s South Texas Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. The flight marked the 15th test flight of Starship since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for SpaceX’s satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket ship still under development. Musk’s space and AI business views Starship as key to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a swarm of orbital AI data-processing centers dubbed Starmind, as the company positions itself to become a high-tech infrastructure provider. SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an upper stage splashing down intact into the Pacific Ocean before bursting into flames. SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot Super Heavy booster three times to its launchpad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such “tower catch” was in March 2025. Musk has said he expects to achieve a pace of weekly Starship launches by the first half of 2027, while SpaceX has said it could begin launching Starship from a new Florida launchpad by the end of 2026. NASA has helped fund Starship’s development with roughly $3.2 billion paid to SpaceX since selecting the rocket ship in 2021 to serve as a lunar lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket’s development. NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing objectives remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth’s orbit to the moon. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA’s Orion capsule, in Earth’s orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA’s planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.

articles.title: Novembro terá superlua no dia 24; veja o que esperar | G1
articles.standfirst: Lua cheia será considerada uma superlua, segundo a Nasa, por ocorrer perto do ponto de maior aproximação da Terra. Astrônoma explica o fenômeno e como observá-lo.
articles.summary: Lua cheia será considerada uma superlua por ocorrer perto do ponto de maior aproximação da Terra. Astrônoma explica o fenômeno e como observá-lo.
articles.body:
Um bando de corvos voa enquanto superlua surge sobre Frankfurt, na Alemanha, em 5 de novembro de 2025. — Foto: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

A Lua cheia de novembro ocorrerá no dia 24, às 11h53, no horário de Brasília , e será considerada uma superlua .

O fenômeno acontece quando a Lua cheia ocorre perto do perigeu , ponto de sua órbita em que o satélite natural fica mais próximo da Terra.

Nessa condição, a Lua pode parecer um pouco maior e mais brilhante do que o habitual.

Segundo a astrônoma Josina Oliveira do Nascimento, do Observatório Nacional (ON) , a Lua estará a aproximadamente 360,8 mil quilômetros da Terra no momento da fase cheia.

A maior aproximação acontecerá no dia seguinte, 25 de novembro, às 18h02.

A Nasa, a agência espacial norte-americana, explica que a superlua de novembro será a primeira de uma sequência de três, que continuará em dezembro e janeiro.

Apesar do nome, porém, a diferença de tamanho nem sempre será facilmente percebida a olho nu.

Fora isso, não existe um critério único para definir uma superlua. Algumas classificações consideram apenas as luas cheias que ocorrem a menos de 360 mil quilômetros da Terra .

Outras exigem que o fenômeno aconteça até 12 horas antes ou depois do perigeu, ponto de maior aproximação do satélite.

Há ainda um terceiro critério, que considera superlua aquela que ocorre quando o satélite está na faixa dos 10% de menor distância da Terra ao longo de sua órbita .

A Lua cheia de 24 de novembro atende apenas a esse último critério. Isso porque estará a 360.768 quilômetros da Terra e ocorrerá cerca de 30 horas antes do perigeu .

Para observar o fenômeno, não será necessário usar telescópios ou binóculos. Como a fase cheia acontecerá durante o dia no Brasil, a melhor oportunidade será depois do pôr do Sol, quando a Lua aparecer no horizonte leste.

"Por questões de ilusão de ótica, quando a gente olha a Lua próxima do horizonte, ela parece ainda maior", explica Josina.

A Nasa ressalta que esse efeito visual também ocorre em luas cheias comuns e não depende da proximidade real do satélite em relação à Terra.

A próxima superlua será em 23 de dezembro, às 22h28, quando a Lua estará a aproximadamente 356,7 mil quilômetros do planeta.

Diferentemente da Lua cheia de novembro, a de dezembro atenderá aos três critérios utilizados para definir uma superlua.

Novembro ainda reserva outros fenômenos para quem gosta de acompanhar o céu. Na madrugada do dia 3, a Lua passa na frente da estrela Regulus , a mais brilhante da constelação de Leão, em parte do Brasil.

Já no dia 7, a Lua minguante e Vênus vão aparecer próximos no céu, pouco antes do amanhecer.

Veja as datas e os horários das principais fases da Lua, no horário de Brasília:

🌗 Quarto minguante (metade da Lua iluminada, com a parte clara diminuindo): ocorreu em 1º de novembro, às 17h28;

🌑 Lua nova (disco praticamente invisível no céu): ocorreu em 9 de novembro, às 4h02;

🌓 Quarto crescente (metade da Lua iluminada, mas com a parte clara aumentando): 17 de novembro, às 8h47;

🌕 Lua cheia (disco lunar totalmente iluminado para quem observa da Terra): 24 de novembro, às 11h53.

❗ Preste atenção no seu fuso, pois os horários mudam de acordo com ele. No Acre, por exemplo, a Lua cheia ocorre às 9h53; em Fernando de Noronha, às 12h53.

Já quem espera um eclipse como o eclipse lunar parcial visto no fim de agosto terá de aguardar: novembro não terá um eclipse do tipo.

O próximo eclipse lunar ocorrerá em fevereiro de 2027 , mas será penumbral e quase imperceptível a olho nu. Um eclipse parcial volta a ser visível em todo o Brasil só em janeiro de 2028 , e um total, em junho de 2029.

A Lua não produz luz própria. O brilho que vemos no céu é a luz do Sol refletida em sua superfície.

Em qualquer momento, metade da Lua está iluminada pelo Sol. O que muda ao longo do seu ciclo então é quanto dessa parte iluminada conseguimos enxergar da Terra, conforme o satélite percorre sua órbita ao redor do planeta.

Na Lua nova, a face iluminada fica voltada principalmente para o lado oposto ao da Terra, e o disco lunar praticamente não aparece no céu. Nos dias seguintes, a parte iluminada visível aumenta.

No quarto crescente , aproximadamente metade do disco que vemos está iluminada. Essa parcela continua aumentando até a Lua cheia , quando praticamente toda a face voltada para a Terra aparece iluminada.

Depois, ocorre o caminho inverso: a área iluminada visível diminui até o quarto minguante e segue encolhendo até uma nova Lua nova.

➡️ O intervalo entre duas luas novas consecutivas é chamado de lunação .

O ciclo que começa em 9 de novembro termina em 8 de dezembro e dura cerca de 29 dias e meio. Por isso, as fases da Lua não acompanham exatamente o começo e o fim dos meses do calendário.

Lua cheia é vista no início do eclipse lunar no Cairo, no Egito, nesta sexta-feira (28). — Foto: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters

A Lua cheia ocorrerá em 24 de novembro , às 11h53 , no horário de Brasília. Como isso acontece durante o dia, o melhor momento para observá-la será depois do pôr do Sol.

Em São Paulo (SP), a Lua nasce por volta das 18h57. No Rio de Janeiro (RJ), às 18h41; em Recife (PE), às 17h33; em Brasília (DF), às 18h44; e em Porto Alegre (RS), às 19h34.

A Lua cheia também será considerada uma superlua , porque ocorrerá quando o satélite estiver próximo do ponto de sua órbita em que fica mais perto da Terra.

No dia 24, a Lua estará a cerca de 361 mil quilômetros do nosso planeta. No dia seguinte, essa distância será ainda menor, de aproximadamente 359 mil quilômetros .

Essa proximidade faz com que a Lua pareça um pouco maior e mais brilhante do que em outras luas cheias.

Ao nascer, próxima ao horizonte, a Lua também poderá parecer maior devido a uma ilusão de ótica e apresentar tons amarelados ou avermelhados por causa da atmosfera.

Imagem feita de Pitangueiras (SP), na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP), por câmera fotográfica de conjunção entre Lua e Vênus. — Foto: José Carlos Salerno

Novembro também será marcado pela chuva de meteoros Leônidas , formada por fragmentos deixados pelo cometa 55P/Tempel-Tuttle .

O fenômeno atinge seu pico em meados do mês, e a melhor oportunidade de observação no Brasil deve ocorrer na madrugada de 18 de novembro.

Em São Paulo (SP), o período mais favorável deve começar por volta das 2h e seguir até pouco antes do amanhecer, quando a constelação de Leão estará mais alta no céu.

Para observar os meteoros, não é necessário usar telescópio ou binóculo. O ideal é procurar um local escuro, longe das luzes das cidades, e observar uma área ampla do céu.

No dia 20 de novembro, Mercúrio poderá ser observado antes do amanhecer, quando atingirá sua maior distância aparente do Sol no céu.

Já no dia 25, Urano estará em uma posição favorável para observação, permanecendo acima do horizonte durante boa parte da noite.

Por ter brilho fraco, porém, será mais fácil encontrá-lo com binóculos ou telescópios .

A luminosidade da Lua, que estará quase cheia, também poderá dificultar a observação do planeta.

articles.title: Beavers were last recorded around Loch Ness in about 1527; nearly 500 years later, Scotland has licensed conservation groups to release up to 15 beaver families into the River Ness catchment over three years.
articles.summary: Every coin has two sides.
articles.body: Every coin has two sides. While human civilisation continues to move forward at a breathtaking pace, driven by trade, industry and technological advancements, somebody else often has to pay the price for it. The natural world has been one of the biggest victims of this progress, with several species being pushed to the brink of extinction. Beavers were among them. Once native to Scotland, these industrious mammals were hunted extensively for their fur, meat and castoreum, a secretion that was highly valued in the perfume trade. Centuries of exploitation eventually wiped them out from the Scottish landscape. Now, nearly 500 years later, they are preparing to make a comeback around Loch Ness.On October 30, 2026, NatureScot, Scotland's nature conservation agency, announced that a licence had been granted to two conservation organisations, Trees for Life and Beaver Trust, to bring beavers back to the River Ness catchment. Under the three-year project, the organisations will be allowed to relocate and release up to 15 beaver families from other parts of Scotland, where they are currently facing conflicts with human activities. The initiative aims to establish a healthy, self-sustaining beaver population in the region while restoring the ecological balance of its rivers and wetlands.Why did beavers disappear from Scotland?Beavers were once a familiar part of Scotland's natural landscape, with their beautiful fur and distinctive appearance, but the very things that made these creatures special also made them victims of human greed. Beavers were once hunted extensively for their thick, waterproof fur, which was highly sought after in Europe. Their pelts were used to make felt hats, which became quite fashionable and turned beaver hunting into a profitable trade. But fur was not the only reason these animals were hunted. Their meat was also consumed, while castoreum, a secretion produced by their scent glands, was valued for its use in perfumes and traditional medicines.Over time, the growing demand for these products took a heavy toll on their population. Their activities also brought them into conflict with humans, as the dams they built could flood agricultural land and interfere with farming. As hunting continued and their natural habitats changed, beaver populations gradually declined until they eventually disappeared from Scotland.Hector Boece, in his History and Chronicles of Scotland, translated by John Bellenden, mentioned beavers as one of the most proficient among the wildlife found in the region around 1526–27. Nearly five centuries later, their presence is once again being planned for the very landscape they once called home.Scotland plans the return of beavers after 500 yearsAs NatureScot announced its three-year conservation plan for the reintroduction of beavers to areas where they once thrived, it granted a licence to two conservation organisations, Trees for Life and Beaver Trust. Under the three-year project, the organisations will be allowed to release up to 15 beaver families in the region. The animals will be relocated from other parts of Scotland, particularly areas where their activities have created conflicts with agricultural land.The initiative, known as the Ness Beaver Project, aims to re-establish a healthy, self-sustaining population of beavers in the region. Before being released, the animals will undergo health checks to ensure they are suitable for relocation. The first releases could begin as early as November 2026, marking an important step in Scotland's efforts to restore its native wildlife.Interestingly, this is not Scotland's first attempt to bring back the species. Beavers were officially reintroduced to the country in 2009 through the Scottish Beaver Trial in Knapdale, Argyll. Their return to the River Ness catchment would extend their presence into another part of their former natural range.How will beavers help restore the ecosystem?Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers, and for good reason. Unlike many other animals, they have the ability to reshape the landscapes around them through their natural activities. By building dams using branches, logs and mud, they slow down the movement of water and create ponds and wetlands. These newly formed habitats provide shelter and breeding grounds for several other species, including fish, amphibians, insects and birds. Their wetlands can also help retain water during dry periods, reduce the impact of flooding by slowing water flows and improve water quality by trapping sediments.Their activities can therefore benefit much more than just their own population. By changing the way water moves through a landscape, beavers help create diverse habitats and support a wider range of wildlife. However, their dams can also create challenges for nearby agricultural land and infrastructure, which makes careful conservation and management important.For Scotland, their planned return to the River Ness catchment is about more than bringing back a species that disappeared centuries ago. It is also an opportunity to restore natural habitats and allow an ecosystem to function with the help of one of its former inhabitants. Nearly 500 years after their disappearance, beavers are preparing to reclaim a place in Scotland's landscape, reminding us that conservation is not simply about protecting what remains, but also about bringing back what we have lost.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Humanity's farthest messenger: Nasa's Voyager 1 nears a one light-day milestone
articles.summary: Imagine sending a message into space and waiting 24 hours just for it to arrive. And if you expect a reply, be prepared to wait another full day.
articles.body: Imagine sending a message into space and waiting 24 hours just for it to arrive. And if you expect a reply, be prepared to wait another full day.That's how far Nasa's Voyager 1 has travelled from Earth. Nearly 49 years after its launch, the spacecraft is approaching an extraordinary milestone that no human-made object has ever achieved, travelling one light-day away from our planet.When it reaches the mark on Wednesday, November 18, even a signal travelling at the speed of light will need an entire day to bridge the distance between Voyager 1 and Earth.More than 26 billion kilometres from Earth, Voyager 1 is travelling at approximately 61,000 km/h. To put that distance into perspective, one light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, covering nearly 25.9 billion kilometres.Even at the speed of light, a signal sent from Earth will take an entire day to reach the spacecraft. A response would take another 24 hours to return, meaning a simple exchange between Nasa and Voyager 1 could take approximately 48 hours.But the distance becomes even more staggering when compared with a light-year. One light-year is approximately 9.46 trillion kilometres. Despite travelling at nearly 61,000 kph, Voyager 1 would need around 18,000 years to cover that distance at its current speed. According to the AP report, it would take more than twice that time before the spacecraft comes near another star.The Voyager 1 milestone is part of one of Nasa's most ambitious space exploration programmes, which began in 1977 with the launch of two robotic spacecraft, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2.The mission was originally designed to study the outer planets of the solar system, particularly Jupiter and Saturn, but a rare alignment of the giant planets allowed Nasa to plan a much wider exploration.According to Nasa, such an alignment occurs roughly once every 175 years and enables spacecraft to use the gravitational pull of planets to change their trajectories and travel towards other destinations. The technique, known as a gravity assist, helped the Voyager spacecraft explore regions of the solar system that had never been studied so closely before.Voyager 1's extraordinary 49-year journeyLaunched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida, Voyager 1 was designed to explore the outer planets of the solar system, but its journey eventually took it far beyond its original mission.The spacecraft first reached Jupiter in March 1979, sending back detailed images and scientific observations of the planet, its atmosphere and moons. Among its major discoveries was active volcanic activity on Io, Jupiter's innermost large moon, marking the first time volcanoes were observed on a world beyond Earth. It also discovered two previously unknown moons, Thebe and Metis, and a thin ring around Jupiter.In November 1980, Voyager 1 flew past Saturn, studying its complex ring system, atmosphere and largest moon, Titan. Its observations of Titan's thick atmosphere provided important insights into one of the most intriguing worlds in the solar system. Having completed its primary planetary mission, the spacecraft continued towards the outer reaches of the solar system.In February 1990, from approximately 6 billion kilometres away, Voyager 1 turned its camera towards Earth and captured the iconic 'Pale Blue Dot' photograph, showing our planet as a tiny speck against the vast darkness of space. The image was later popularised by astronomer Carl Sagan, who was part of the mission's imaging team. NASA subsequently switched off the spacecraft's cameras to conserve power.On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's influence through the solar wind gives way to the interstellar environment. It became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space.Nearly 49 years after its launch, the spacecraft continues to travel farther into the galaxy, sending scientific measurements back to Earth and preparing to achieve another historic first by reaching one light-day from our planetYour child uses AI every day. articles.title: Second catch attempt for SpaceX Starship rocket
articles.summary: The attempt follows an unsuccessful effort to catch of the rocket’s booster which instead came down in the ocean.
articles.body:
SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 1515 local time (2115GMT) on Saturday.

This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1647 local time (2147GMT) on Friday.

The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.

A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.

During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely."

The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.

The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the "chopsticks".

Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.

If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.

In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.

Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.

But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society.

"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.

"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."

After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa.

The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.

SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown.

Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule.

Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage.

Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.

Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title: Elon Musk se queda sin la doble captura de Starship tras la explosión del propulsor de SpaceX
articles.standfirst: El fallo durante el aterrizaje en el Golfo de México frustra uno de los objetivos más ambiciosos de la compañía
articles.summary: El fallo durante el aterrizaje en el Golfo de México frustra uno de los objetivos más ambiciosos de la compañía
articles.body: El proyecto de Elon Musk para recuperar completamente el cohete Starship ha sufrido otro revés. El superpropulsor de SpaceX explotó cuando cayó en el Golfo de México el viernes y no completó la doble captura que la compañía había preparado para su prueba más ambiciosa hasta la fecha. La nave espacial entró en órbita pero continuó con el desarrollo de la misión. El incidente es una mala noticia para los planes de Musk de hacer de Starship un vehículo completamente reutilizable. Quería que ambas etapas del cohete fueran recuperadas usando los brazos mecánicos montados en la torre de lanzamiento en Starbase, Texas: se suponía que el propulsor regresaría a la plataforma después del despegue, pero en su lugar fue a un área marítima donde explotó. La compañía no había comunicado la causa del fallo. Sin esta primera etapa era imposible alcanzar uno de los hitos principales planeados para el vuelo (el resto de la operación continuó). Starship aún logró entrar en órbita y desplegó 26 de los satélites Starlink más avanzados de la compañía. Luego hará 15 órbitas alrededor de la Tierra (a unos 275 km de altitud) antes de regresar a la plataforma de lanzamiento. La maniobra estaba programada para el sábado y podría extender el vuelo hasta 22 horas. La prueba es también el primer intento de capturar la versión mejorada del propulsor (de 72 m de largo) que se utilizará para futuras misiones a la Luna y Marte. La nave espacial mide otros 52 m de altura, por lo que todo el conjunto mide 124 m de alto. SpaceX ya lo había hecho tres veces antes, pero nunca dos veces. Para Musk, eso sería un gran paso hacia un sistema de lanzamiento reutilizable rápido necesario para sus planes de construir bases en la luna y enviar humanos a Marte. Durante la transmisión, la comentarista Kate Tice resumió el contratiempo: “Bueno, ciertamente no son las noticias que esperábamos escuchar hoy.”

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day
articles.summary: The probe was launched in 1977, and it continues to relay space-related data back to a team of NASA scientists.
articles.body:
NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.

On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.

The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.

NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.

Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.

Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.

Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.

In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.

Voyager 1 project manager Suzanne Dodd described Voyager 1 as “a national treasure” and told The Associated Press news agency that the two probes’ activities are akin to that of weather satellites.

The probe’s cultural impact has been significant. The famous “Pale Blue Dot” photo of Earth was taken by Voyager 1 in 1990.

“All of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement.

articles.title: Scientists surveyed two remote Pacific atolls and found 15 seabird species confirmed or likely to be breeding, 132 turtle nest pits and two fish observations requiring further study; the atolls provide a benchmark for a 48,000-square-kilometre sanctuary
articles.summary: Some of the world's healthiest marine ecosystems may still exist in places so remote that human activity has had little influence on their wildlife and
articles.body: Some of the world's healthiest marine ecosystems may still exist in places so remote that human activity has had little influence on their wildlife and habitats. Scientists surveying two isolated Pacific atolls have documented thriving seabird colonies, green sea turtle nesting grounds, diverse fish communities and extensive coral reefs. The findings offer a rare picture of what relatively undisturbed tropical ocean ecosystems can look like.The findings come from a study published on November 11, 2026, in Frontiers in Marine Science, titled From the sky to the deep sea: ecosystem structure and ecological integrity across the National Marine Sanctuaries of Bikar and Bokak, Marshall Islands. The research, led by marine ecologist Dr Alan Friedlander of the University of Hawai'i, examined ecosystems across two remote atolls in the Marshall Islands. The assessment also provides an ecological benchmark for the country's first national marine sanctuaries, covering approximately 48,136 square kilometres around the islands.Two remote atolls with thriving wildlifeThe researchers studied Bikar and Bokak, the northernmost atolls in the Republic of the Marshall Islands. Both are uninhabited and geographically isolated from major population centres. Bikar lies approximately 116 kilometres from Utrik, the nearest inhabited atoll, while Bokak is around 385 kilometres away. Their remoteness has helped preserve ecosystems that have experienced relatively little direct human pressure.The research team conducted an extensive expedition in 2023 in collaboration with the Marshall Islands Marine Resources Authority and National Geographic's Pristine Seas programme. Scientists examined habitats from the islands' vegetation and seabird colonies to shallow coral reefs, deeper underwater environments and the open ocean.Their methods included scuba surveys, underwater video recordings, deep-sea camera deployments, vegetation assessments and observations from a submersible. The aim was to understand how different habitats function together rather than studying coral reefs in isolation.Seabird colonies, turtle nests and potential new speciesThe survey recorded 17 seabird species across the two atolls, of which 15 were confirmed or considered likely to be breeding. Researchers also recorded 132 sea turtle nest pits, the majority attributed to green sea turtles, with nesting activity concentrated almost entirely at Bikar. The underwater surveys revealed considerable fish diversity. Scientists documented 266 reef fish taxa, 138 fish taxa during deeper-water submersible surveys and 79 deep-sea vertebrate taxa. They also recorded 15 pelagic fish taxa, including sharks, jacks, wahoo and other open-water species.Fourteen of the fish taxa recorded during the submersible surveys appear to represent previously unreported records for the Marshall Islands. Two other observations were provisionally identified as belonging to the genera Dactylanthias and Parapercis, but require further taxonomic confirmation. These findings highlight how much remains to be explored in the region's deeper marine environments. The researchers also identified differences between the two atolls. Bokak supported greater reef-fish biomass and had more coral-dominated reef communities. Bikar, meanwhile, had greater macroalgal cover, more extensive native Pisonia grandis forests and higher sea turtle nesting activity.The study did not establish exactly why these ecological differences exist. Factors such as lagoon size, water movement, sediment transport, nutrient availability and habitat structure could contribute to the variations.A 48,136-square-kilometre sanctuaryThe research was intended to support conservation planning under the Marshall Islands' Reimaanlok framework, a community-led approach to protecting marine and terrestrial resources. The recently established National Marine Sanctuaries of Bikar and Bokak cover approximately 48,136 square kilometres. The study provides an ecological baseline to support their long-term monitoring and conservation under the Reimaanlok Framework.According to Friedlander, these atolls offer valuable reference points for understanding marine ecosystems that have experienced limited human influence. Their ecological conditions can help scientists understand what has been lost in more heavily affected environments and guide future conservation and restoration efforts.Why the findings matterThe researchers said relatively undisturbed ecosystems are becoming increasingly rare as marine environments face pressures from climate change, overexploitation and pollution. They emphasised that conservation studies should examine entire ecosystems, from terrestrial vegetation and seabird colonies to shallow reefs and deep-sea habitats. Focusing only on shallow coral reefs can overlook important ecological connections between different environments. The team also identified areas for future research, including how nutrients move between habitats and how species interact across different depths.The findings establish an important baseline against which future environmental changes can be measured. They also demonstrate the conservation value of protecting large, interconnected marine environments before human pressures significantly alter their ecological balance.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: When people entered a cave in Chiapas, Mexico, in 2012, they found 165 human skulls from a 1,000-year-old Maya skull rack; experts now say about half belonged to women and 15 to children, not just male war captives
articles.summary: Not all findings in history lead us to an answer; some leave us grappling with even more questions.
articles.body: Not all findings in history lead us to an answer; some leave us grappling with even more questions. Human remains have long opened up a range of curious questions: what happened, why, and who were these people? More often than not, they open the pathway for researchers to learn what beliefs and traditions shaped community life and even death.But sometimes, what appears to be a familiar archaeological finding can turn out to tell a rather different story. This was the case with a collection of 165 human skulls discovered inside a cave in Chiapas, Mexico, in 2012. At first associated with the ancient Maya practice of displaying human skulls, the remains have now offered researchers a more complicated picture of the people who were part of these ceremonies, with women and children forming a significant part of this collection.A discovery inside a cave in ChiapasAccording to findings from Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), reported by Arkeonews on November 6, 2026, the discovery was made in the Frontera Comalapa region of Chiapas, close to Mexico's border with Guatemala. When the human skulls were first encountered inside the cave in 2012, their presence raised questions about the circumstances in which they had been brought together. Ensuing investigations by INAH, established that the remains belonged to people who lived approximately 1,000 years ago, during the Early Postclassic period, between AD 900 and 1200.The collection was identified as a tzompantli, a structure associated with the ceremonial display or arrangement of human skulls in ancient Mesoamerican societies. These structures are perhaps most widely associated with the Aztec civilisation, particularly the large skull displays found in the ancient city of Tenochtitlan. However, the Frontera Comalapa discovery is considerably older than the famous skull altars of central Mexico, adding another dimension to what researchers understand about the practice.According to INAH's announcement dated October 28, 2026, researchers have now established that the collection contains 165 skulls. Of these, 15 belonged to children, while 83 were identified as belonging to women and 79 to men. The sex of the remaining three individuals could not be determined because their skulls were too fragmented. The nearly equal representation of women and men in this particular collection, however, suggests that the people represented in these ancient ceremonies may have come from a much wider group than previously assumed.What the skulls revealed about the peopleDetermining the sex of the individuals was not straightforward, as the researchers did not have pelvic bones available for examination. The pelvis is generally considered the most reliable skeletal indicator for estimating biological sex. Instead, researchers examined differences in the skulls, including the shape of the lower jaw and the bony structures above the eye sockets.The initial investigations were undertaken by physical anthropologist Javier Montes de Paz, while the subsequent estimations were carried out by researchers Cristell Delesma Pérez and Abigail Reyes López. The ages of the individuals also offer an interesting glimpse into the population represented in the cave. Most of the adults were estimated to have been between 25 and 35 years old when they died. However, researchers have also identified two individuals who were perhaps roughly between 55 and 70 years of age.Researchers also identified cut marks on the remains of three individuals, while some of the bones showed evidence of exposure to heat. Soot deposits were also observed on the cave's ceiling. Together, these findings suggest that fire may have been used inside the cave, possibly by people entering with torches to carry out ceremonies.Lozada Toledo suggested that the cave could have been a place of pilgrimage for nearby Maya communities, where people gathered for different religious practices, possibly also including ceremonies seeking rainfall. However, these findings require further exploration. For instance, the cut marks and evidence of heat exposure do not independently establish that all the individuals were sacrificed.The significance of a skull beyond its physical formAnother fascinating aspect of the discovery lies in the way the remains appear to have been treated after death. Researchers found that most of the skulls were missing their lower jaws, while the teeth had also been removed from the upper jaws. Some showed evidence of intentional cranial deformation, a practice carried out during childhood by using boards to influence the developing shape of the head.The collection also contained 51 long bones, alongside the 165 skulls. Their preservation has allowed researchers to identify even some of the smaller skeletal structures. One particularly remarkable example was the survival of a malleus, also known as the hammer bone, in the middle ear of an individual. Measuring approximately 8 to 9 millimetres, this tiny bone is not commonly preserved in archaeological contexts.These details have led researchers to consider whether the remains were handled, removed and repositioned more than once as part of ceremonial practices. The skulls may therefore represent more than a single event or a straightforward collection of victims.According to INAH, Lozada Toledo has also pointed towards the spiritual significance attached to different parts of the human body in Mesoamerican belief systems. The head, in particular, was associated with tonalli, suggesting a person's essence. The findings as a whole reveal the distinct nature of rituals that must have carried meanings extending beyond the physical display of human remains.Your child uses AI every day.
